audit.dimension: Mathematics and statistics (mathematics.md, statistical parts of design.md / protocol.md / from-zero-lab.md / experiment-plan.md / strategy-dossier.md, counterexamples.json, lab-spec.json, records.schema.json)
audit.verdict_summary: Where the documents state formulas, the formulas are almost always right. The anytime Hoeffding band, its pi^2 n^2/(3 delta) constant, the union bounds over K and over an open stream (delta_i = 6 delta/(pi^2 i^2)), the counterexample arithmetic, the Borel-Cantelli point about archive revisits, the law-of-total-expectation survivor argument, the knowledge-gradient VOI and the zero-failure binomial bound all check out, and the caveats are honest. The machinery is still not ready to make decisions. The only formal rule (Hoeffding-band dormancy) does nothing at feasible sample sizes: it is plus or minus 43 points at n=30, against about 11 for a variance-adaptive betting confidence sequence and about 5.5 for a fixed-n t-interval at SD 15. The primary estimand leaves out the per-run token-efficiency term, which is capped at 50 for early exits, so finishing all 48 months is worth about 5 Stage-1 points on top of quantitative_score. Two validity conditions that bear directly on problem B are missing: launch-order indexing under asynchronous completion (failures return first) and informative operational censoring (long episodes are more exposed to crashes). The cheap-vs-target calibration pilot (6 policies x 2 actors x 3 episodes) is about an order of magnitude too small: the 95% CI for r=0.6 is [-0.41, 0.95] and per-cell reliability is about 0.46. The documents never turn the official max-over-at-most-3-scored-versions rule into a decision, even though three distinct equal-mean versions are worth about +5.9 Stage-1 points in expectation at SD 15. That rule also means version-level variance has positive option value at submission time, while it stays a nuisance for estimating means. Multiplicity is framed only as FWER union bounds. What the lab needs instead is partial-pooling shrinkage for selection, e-BH/e-LOND FDR for screening, and fresh frozen confirmation with a concurrent incumbent for claims. Method evaluation (baselines, ablations, reopening quotas) has no feasible replication design, which a replay testbed with common random numbers would supply.

errors.claim: Primary outcome = mean terminal quantitative_score (Y = quantitative_score/100) under the target actor.
errors.problem: Under the official formula the per-run objective also contains 0.1 x token efficiency. That term is computed per run and capped at 50 if the run ends before month 48, so completion and tokens per month change the version score directly. Two policies with equal mean Q but different completion rates (or different context growth) have different expected Stage-1 scores. Completing versus failing is worth up to 5 Stage-1 points, about 6.25 Q-points, beyond any effect on Q.
errors.correction: Primary per-episode outcome Y = 0.8*Q + 0.1*E_run, where E_run = min(cap_T, clip(100*(3e6 - tokens/T)/2.5e6, 0, 100)), cap_T = 50 if T<48 else 100 (Y in [0,90]; the 0.1*D Skill-quality term is constant per version). If the target pilot shows <=500k tokens/month, Y = 0.8Q + 5 + 5*1[T=48]. Non-target actors (whose token counts are meaningless) use the proxy Y' = 0.8Q + 0.1*E_hat(C), with E_hat taken from the target pilot. Report Q, completion and E separately as auxiliaries.

errors.claim: Anytime Hoeffding band b_i(n)=sqrt(log(pi^2 n^2/(3 delta_i))/(2n)) (x100 for [0,100]) with the dormancy rule 'upper bound below a contender's lower bound'.
errors.problem: The derivation is correct, but the rule cannot fire at budgets this lab can afford. The band ignores variance (it assumes the worst-case SD of 50 points for [0,100]). Half-widths at delta=0.05: n=10: 66 (K=1) / 77 (K=20) points; n=30: 43 / 48; n=100: 26 / 29. Two arms are separated only if their means differ by more than about 85 points at n=30. The docs admit the bands are 'muy anchas' but keep the rule as the only formal dormancy criterion.
errors.correction: Do not use Hoeffding union bands for decisions. For anytime-valid claims use variance-adaptive confidence sequences: the hedged-capital betting CS (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2024), about plus or minus 11 points at n=30 and SD 15 in my simulation, or PrPl-EB, closed-form but loose below n of about 20. Make reversible decisions with a calibrated Bayesian posterior rule. If only a few pre-planned looks are used, a union over L looks (alpha/L) is much tighter than a union over all n.

errors.claim: The band 'tolera mirar repetidamente' under independent episodes from a stable distribution; asynchrony is handled qualitatively by 'rondas comparables'.
errors.problem: The time-uniform guarantee holds for each arm's outcome sequence only when the indexing order is independent of the outcomes (the 'stack of rewards' argument). With parallel workers, early failures finish first. If means or CS are updated in completion order, the running estimate of a fresh policy is biased low while its successful episodes are still running. The bias falls on late-benefit policies, which is problem B. Sample means under adaptive allocation are also biased in their own right: negative for a fixed arm (Nie et al. 2018), of either sign under adaptive stopping/choice (Shin, Ramdas & Rinaldo 2019). No estimator or data-inclusion rule is specified.
errors.correction: Assign a launch index k per cell and interleave arms in launch blocks. Decisions use only the prefix-complete set n_c = max{k : launches 1..k resolved}; later results are stored but frozen out until the prefix closes. Pending jobs never enter estimators. Claims about the selected policy come only from fresh, non-adaptively allocated confirmation data.

errors.claim: Administrative interruption is 'censored, not a score'; no terminal score is imputed.
errors.problem: Labelling is correct, but no estimator or sensitivity analysis is defined. Complete-case analysis is biased whenever interruption risk grows with episode length. A 48-month run makes roughly 8x the tool and LLM calls of a 6-month failure, so rate limits and timeouts preferentially remove good episodes. That is informative censoring, and it biases means downward, most for the best policies.
errors.correction: (1) First try to resume the same session via observe (flag resumed=true; sensitivity analysis excludes resumed episodes). (2) Otherwise mark it censored and launch a replacement in the same block. (3) Report Manski-type bounds with censored Y set to 0 and to 90 (or the cell min/max). If a decision flips between the bounds, record 'inconclusive' and run another block. (4) Alarm if censoring exceeds 10% in a cell or the censoring-rate ratio between compared arms exceeds 2.

errors.claim: Variability only misleads ('The highest observed score prefers variability'). The scoring consequences listed are linear in the mean.
errors.problem: For estimating mu this is right, but it misses how the official objective is built. Stage 1 = max over at most three scored versions (the latest unscored version at each of three cutoffs). Content-identical versions are not rescored, and a lower later score never reduces Stage 1. The version score has SD of about 0.8*sigma/sqrt(3) (6.9 Stage-1 points at sigma_Q=15). Then E[max of 2 equal-mean versions] = m + 0.564*s (+3.9) and E[max of 3] = m + 0.846*s (+5.9), which is comparable to a 7-Q-point policy improvement. Version-level variance therefore has positive option value in the submission decision (expected improvement over the best issued score, or P(exceed top-10 boundary)). None of the documents quantifies this or turns it into a rule.
errors.correction: Keep mu as the estimand for search and ranking, but add a pre-registered submission rule. Submit a distinct, valid, genuinely revised version at every cutoff (27 Oct, 30 Oct, 1 Nov, 24:00 GMT). Choose each one by EI = (m - A*)Phi(z) + s phi(z), with s^2 = 0.64(sigma_v^2/3 + posterior var) + omega_env^2. Example with A*=50: a policy with m=46 and s=10 has EI 2.3, double the 1.15 of m=48 and s=5.

errors.claim: Six policies x two actors x three episodes per cell (36 episodes) is a pilot; then 'Comprobar acuerdo de ranking y falsos descartes'.
errors.problem: The design cannot measure the things it is asked to check. With K=6 policies, the Fisher 95% CI for an observed Pearson r=0.6 is [-0.41, 0.95] (K=10: [-0.05, 0.89]; K=20: [0.21, 0.82]). With n=3 episodes per cell, per-cell reliability tau^2/(tau^2+sigma^2/n) is about 0.46 (tau=8, sigma=15), so even a perfect true correlation is observed at roughly half its size. False-rejection audits built from a handful of target episodes give Clopper-Pearson upper bounds of about 45-60%. The 'pilot' label is honest, but the protocol then lets this pilot decide pruning authority.
errors.correction: Make calibration a by-product: every policy evaluated on the target also gets at least 6 screening-actor episodes in the same epoch. Use at least 8-10 shared policies spanning at least 20 Q-points, including deliberate anchors (minimal, safety-first, growth-first, scripted-legal). Fit a bivariate errors-in-variables hierarchical model rather than correlating raw cell means. Grant pruning authority only under the explicit criteria in the protocol, and report decision-focused metrics (top-k recall, regret of the cheap-selected policy, randomized-audit false-rejection rate).

errors.claim: Distinguishing two means separated by Delta costs 'del orden de varianza / Delta^2' samples.
errors.problem: The order is right, but the constants are large and drive the budget. Two-sample n per arm = 2(z_alpha+z_beta)^2 sigma^2/Delta^2, which is about 9 sigma^2/Delta^2 (one-sided alpha=0.10, 80% power) to 15.7 sigma^2/Delta^2 (two-sided 0.05). Best-arm identification adds a log(1/delta) factor (Kaufmann et al. 2016). At sigma=15, a 5-point difference needs about 82-142 episodes per arm and a 10-point difference about 21-36, not about 9.
errors.correction: State n = ceil(2(z_{1-alpha}+z_{1-beta})^2 sigma_U^2/Delta^2), with sigma_U an upper-80% chi-square bound on the pooled SD, re-estimated each block (internal pilot).

errors.claim: 'usar factoriales sólo cuando la interacción sea la pregunta' (one change at a time otherwise).
errors.problem: This gets the efficiency argument backwards. At equal total N, a 2x2 factorial estimates each main effect with variance 4sigma^2/N, against 6sigma^2/N for a 3-arm one-factor-at-a-time design (1.5x more efficient, through hidden replication). The interaction contrast is the expensive part (SE 2sigma/sqrt(m) against sigma/sqrt(m) for a main effect), so it needs about 4x the per-cell n.
errors.correction: Use 2x2 factorials by default for two plausible, roughly additive changes, and analyse main effects first. Treat the interaction as exploratory unless per-cell n is large.
evidence: Box, Hunter & Hunter, Statistics for Experimenters (2nd ed., 2005), ch. 5

errors.claim: r_simple = max_i mu_i,obj,e - mu_hat,obj,e
errors.problem: Simple regret must use the TRUE mean of the returned policy, mu_{p_hat}, not its estimate. Plugging in the estimate of the selected policy inherits the optimizer's curse: the estimate is biased upward after selection.
errors.correction: r_simple = max_i mu_i - mu_{p_hat}. Estimate it only with fresh confirmation data, or with shrinkage or winner's-curse-corrected intervals (Andrews, Kitagawa & McCloskey 2024).

errors.claim: mu_obj(p) = a_m(x_p) + b_m(x_p) mu_m(p) + residual as a calibration hypothesis.
errors.problem: Fitted on estimated cell means, this is an errors-in-variables regression. The slope is attenuated by the reliability of the cheap-actor means (about 0.46 at n=3, tau=8, sigma=15), so target differences are systematically under-predicted and the residual variance is overstated.
errors.correction: Fit a bivariate hierarchical model with known measurement-error variances (sigma_a^2/n), or Deming regression. Report the posterior of rho and the slope, plus the predictive interval for a new policy.

errors.claim: Illustrative table: A (30 games, SE 0.5), B (10 games, SE 4), C (30 games, SE 1).
errors.problem: The implied per-episode SDs are 2.7 (A), 12.6 (B) and 5.5 (C). An SD of 2.7 is implausibly small for a stochastic LLM-driven 48-month game, and the SDs are mutually inconsistent, so the lesson 'A is stable' mixes up SD and n.

errors.claim: hijos_permitidos = max(2, floor(k (1+visitas)^alpha)), alpha example 0.5, k unspecified.
errors.problem: The form matches standard progressive widening, but k is unspecified, alpha is unjustified, and 'visits' is undefined. Infinitely-many-armed bandit theory ties the exponent to the reservoir tail. UCB-AIR adds a new arm when K_{n-1} < n^{beta/(beta+1)} (for beta>=1 or mu*=1), where P(mu_new > mu* - eps) = Theta(eps^beta), so alpha=0.5 implicitly assumes beta=1. LLM mutation children are not i.i.d. reservoir draws, so even that link is only heuristic.
errors.correction: Set k=1, visits = terminal episodes in the family subtree, and alpha = beta_hat/(beta_hat+1), with beta_hat estimated from the upper tail of observed child-minus-parent improvements (default 1). Keep a generation floor (for example 20% of screening episodes) and label the rule a heuristic.
evidence: Wang, Audibert, Munos, NIPS 2008 (UCB-AIR rule and Theorem 4), https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2008/hash/49ae49a23f67c759bf4fc791ba842aa2-Abstract.html

recommendations.recommendation: Adopt Y = 0.8*Q + 0.1*E_run (target actor) as the single pre-registered primary outcome. Use the proxy Y' = 0.8Q + 0.1*E_hat(completion) for non-target actors, and report Q, completion rate (Clopper-Pearson), Kaplan-Meier survival, CVaR20(Y), tokens/month, USD/episode, invalid actions and ending-dimension contributions as auxiliaries.
recommendations.rationale: This matches the official per-run objective, including the completion-dependent efficiency cap (up to 5 Stage-1 points). Decisions follow one quantity; auxiliaries are for diagnosis only.

recommendations.recommendation: Enforce launch-indexed, block-interleaved, prefix-complete data rules. Handle operational censoring by resume-by-observe, same-block replacement, Manski bounds and alarms (censoring >10% per cell or rate ratio >2).
recommendations.rationale: Without these rules, the order in which episodes finish and the timing of operational failures bias estimates against long, late-benefit episodes (problem B), and no confidence band is valid.

recommendations.recommendation: Use two inference layers. (1) A Bayesian hierarchical partial-pooling model per actor and family drives all reversible decisions (allocation, dormancy, promotion), with thresholds pre-registered and their operating characteristics checked by simulation against a pilot-fitted bounded mixture. (2) Anytime-valid hedged betting confidence sequences and e-processes (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2024; Ramdas et al. 2023) support claims and irreversible actions. Drop Hoeffding union bands as an operational rule.
recommendations.rationale: Decisions should maximise expected score, while claims need error control. Shrinkage removes most of the winner's curse: with 20 equal candidates, n=4 and sigma=15, the raw maximum overstates by about 14 points, about 4 after shrinkage with tau=5. Betting confidence sequences are about 4x tighter than Hoeffding at n=30.

recommendations.recommendation: Adopt an explicit submission rule. Submit a distinct, genuinely revised valid version at every cutoff (the first is 27 Oct 24:00 GMT, tomorrow). Choose later versions by expected improvement over the best issued score, using predictive SD^2 = 0.64(sigma_v^2/3 + posterior var) + omega_env^2. If a public leaderboard reveals the top-10 boundary T, maximise P(max >= T) instead.
recommendations.rationale: Stage 1 is the max over at most three scored versions, so extra draws add about +3.9 (two versions) or +5.9 (three versions) Stage-1 points in expectation at sigma=15, and the choice among versions depends on variance.

recommendations.recommendation: Size samples from observed variability. Pilot n0=4 episodes (screening) or 3 (target); sigma_U = upper-80% chi-square bound on the pooled SD; n/arm = ceil(9.02*sigma_U^2/Delta^2); re-estimate after every block. Set Delta_s=4 Y-points for screening and Delta_t=8 for target replacement claims. Stop estimating a finalist's absolute mean once n_t>=12 (lab SE no more than half the official 3-run SE).
recommendations.rationale: Precision should be tied to what the official 3-run noise and the budget can resolve. At sigma=15, Delta=4-5 is resolvable only on cheap actors, and Delta of about 8-10 only on target.

recommendations.recommendation: Confirm on held-out data after freezing. Freeze at most 2 finalists plus the incumbent; run fixed-n interleaved target blocks with a single look (or at most 3 looks with O'Brien-Fleming boundaries 3.471/2.454/2.004); primary test is a Welch one-sided 95% bound with Bonferroni alpha/2, with a hedged-CS sensitivity analysis. Never reuse confirmation data for selection, and report exploration-stage effects with winner's-curse corrections.
recommendations.rationale: This removes the selection and adaptive-sampling bias and protects against drift. A single frozen candidate without a concurrent control cannot confirm an improvement.

recommendations.recommendation: Redesign calibration and audits. Every target-evaluated policy also gets at least 6 screening episodes; use at least 8 shared policies spanning at least 20 Q-points; fit a bivariate errors-in-variables model. Grant pruning authority only if P(rho>0.5)>=0.8 and no audited false rejections. Audit dormant candidates at random (q=0.2 per block, seeded and logged), estimate the false-rejection rate by IPW with Clopper-Pearson bounds, and revoke authority on the first false rejection among the first 5 audits.
recommendations.rationale: Problem A cannot be settled with 6x3 cells. Calibration has to be measured on the decisions it affects, and false rejections can only be estimated without bias through randomised audits.

recommendations.recommendation: Treat screening multiplicity as an FDR problem. Use e-processes against the incumbent on block-paired differences, Z_k=(Y_A - Y_B + 90)/180 with H0: E[Z] <= (Delta+90)/180. Apply e-BH at q=0.10 per batch (reject the k largest e-values, where k is the largest index with e_(k) >= K/(q k)), or e-LOND online. Reserve FWER (Bonferroni) for the at most 2-3 confirmatory claims.
recommendations.rationale: FWER union bounds are too strict for a stream of 50-200 candidates. e-BH is valid under arbitrary dependence and optional stopping, and e-LOND handles an open candidate set without pre-registering K.

recommendations.recommendation: Evaluate the method on a replay testbed: a frozen catalog of at least 30 policies with at least 30 episodes each, common random numbers across methods, R>=30 searches per method at equal budget. Compare uniform plus pick-best, successive halving, Best-of-N without feedback, refine-leader, the full method, and ablations (no reopening, archive quota 0/5/10%, no calibration, no diversity, no specialisation). Score simple regret, probability of selecting within Delta_s of the best, false-dormancy rate and cost, using paired Wilcoxon tests.
recommendations.rationale: This is the only affordable way to give the method-versus-baselines and ablation requirements statistical power. Live LLM searches are n=1-2 case studies.

recommendations.recommendation: For late benefits and deceptive specialisation: no pruning on partial episodes; use a partial-episode proxy only after leave-one-family-out validation on completed episodes from at least 10 policies (Kendall tau >= 0.7, no top-3 false rejection); compare complete policies by intention-to-treat; add a randomised switch-month negative control (M ~ U{5..12} assigned at launch) for calendar rules.
recommendations.rationale: Bad policies already end early (random play survives 5.9 months on average), so truncation saves little and mainly risks discarding slow starters. Randomising the switch month separates a calendar effect from state accumulation and survivor selection.

recommendations.recommendation: Tie progressive widening to an estimated reservoir exponent: alpha = beta_hat/(beta_hat+1), k=1, visits = terminal episodes in the subtree, with a 20% generation floor. Base family potential on the shrinkage-estimated distribution of child-minus-parent improvements (expected improvement of the next m children), explicitly labelled a heuristic.
recommendations.rationale: This gives the constants a principled source without claiming bounds on descendants.

recommendations.recommendation: Run a sentinel incumbent in every block, test for drift (CUSUM, or early-versus-late two-sample test at p<0.01), and include route or alias in the epoch key.
recommendations.rationale: Changes in target-model hosting or alias break the stationarity every interval assumes.

recommendations.recommendation: Extend records.schema.json with launch_index, block_id, analysis_role, prereg_protocol_id, total_tokens, efficiency_score, resumed, route_id and dimension_contributions, and have the integrator enforce role separation.

recommendations.recommendation: Ask the organisers whether development episodes may use the same designated model (deepseek-v4-flash) through a personally funded, non-competition key or provider.

Third-party aggregators list about USD 0.07-0.14 per million input tokens (unverified), and the competition key's USD 50 likely buys only about 13-110 full episodes.

audit.concrete_protocol:
PRE-REGISTERED STATISTICAL PROTOCOL v0. Freeze this text and its hash before any lab episode. Any amendment gets a new protocol id and starts a new epoch.

0. CELLS. Cell c = (policy sha256 p, actor a, epoch e).
- Actor a = model id or alias, plus harness (JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 agent | Claude Code CLI 2.1.303 with flags | scripted vX), wrapper-prompt hash and effort/temperature.
- Epoch e = engine/dataset versions, runner revision, protocol id, provider route if observable, and calendar block.
- Never pool across cells except through the models in sections 4 and 8.

1. OUTCOMES.
- Per terminal episode: Q in [0,100]; T = months survived; C = 1[T=48]; E = min(cap_T, clip(100*(3e6 - tokens/T)/2.5e6, 0, 100)), with cap_T = 50 if T<48, else 100.
- PRIMARY: Y = 0.8Q + 0.1E in [0,90], on the target actor.
- Non-target actors: Y' = 0.8Q + 0.1*E_hat(C), where E_hat(0)=50 and E_hat(1) = mean E of target completions. If the target stays at or below 500k tokens/month, Y' = 0.8Q + 5 + 5C.
- AUXILIARY (descriptive only): completion rate (Clopper-Pearson), Kaplan-Meier survival, mean Q, CVaR20%(Y), per-policy SD sigma_p, tokens/month, USD/episode, invalid actions and tool errors, official ending-dimension contributions.
- Only Y drives decisions. sigma_p enters only the submission rule (section 9).

2. DATA INCLUSION.
(a) Each launch gets a launch index k within its cell and a block id. Each block interleaves the compared arms (A,B,A,B,...).
(b) Decisions use only the prefix-complete set, n_c = max{k : launches 1..k resolved}.
(c) Pending jobs are never observations.
(d) Operational failure: first try to resume the same session via observe (resumed=true). Otherwise mark the episode censored and launch a replacement in the same block.
- Primary analysis = complete cases. Sensitivity = Manski bounds, with censored Y set to 0 and to 90 (or the cell min and max). If the decision flips between bounds, record 'inconclusive' and run another block.
- Alarms: censoring >10% in a cell; censoring-rate ratio >2 between compared arms; censoring concentrated in long episodes.

3. PILOT AND VARIANCE.
- New candidate: n0 = 4 terminal episodes on the screening actor; n0_t = 3 on the target.
- Pooled within-actor variance s_a^2 with df nu = sum(n_p - 1). Planning SD sigma_U = s_a*sqrt(nu/chi2_{0.20,nu}).
- Re-estimate after every block (internal pilot).
- Target cost pilot: 2 episodes give mean cost c_bar. Target budget N_t = floor(0.9*remaining_USD/c_bar).
- Budget split: 15% calibration/audit, 45% finalist selection, 30% confirmation, 10% reserve. If N_t < 20: no calibration study, at most 2 finalists, and cheap actors only screen gross failures.

4. DECISION MODEL (Bayesian partial pooling, per actor).
- Model: Y_pj ~ N(mu_p, sigma_a^2); mu_p ~ N(m_f, tau_a^2) within family f.
- tau_hat^2 = max(9, Var_w(ybar_p) - mean(s^2/n_p)), i.e. a 3-point floor (DerSimonian-Laird style).
- Posterior: mu~_p = m_f + B_p(ybar_p - m_f), with B_p = tau^2/(tau^2 + sigma^2/n_p) and v_p = B_p*sigma^2/n_p.
- Robustness: refit with Student-t (nu=4) errors and with a Bayesian bootstrap. Any decision that flips between fits is 'inconclusive'.
- Calibrate all thresholds below by simulation from a bounded mixture fitted to pilot data. Targets: false dormancy of within-Delta_s policies <= 10%; probability of correct selection reported.

5. ANYTIME-VALID LAYER (claims and irreversible acts).
- Per cell, the hedged-capital CS (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2024) on X = Y/90, alpha = 0.05:
  - lam~_t = sqrt(2 log(2/alpha)/(sig2_{t-1}*t*log(1+t))); lam+_t(m) = min(lam~_t, c/m); lam-_t(m) = min(lam~_t, c/(1-m)); c = 0.5; theta = 0.5.
  - K_t(m) = max(theta*prod(1 + lam+(X_i - m)), (1-theta)*prod(1 - lam-(X_i - m))).
  - CS_t = {m : K_t(m) < 1/alpha}, intersected over time.
  - sig2_t = (1/4 + sum (X_i - mu_i)^2)/(t+1); mu_t = (1/2 + sum X_i)/(t+1).
- Two-arm comparisons use block-paired Z_k = (Y_Ak - Y_Bk + 90)/180.
- e-process for H0: mu_A - mu_B <= Delta: W_t = prod_k (1 + lam_k(Z_k - m0)), with m0 = (Delta+90)/180 and predictable lam_k in [0, c/m0). Reject when W_t >= 1/alpha (Ville).
- Screening multiplicity: e-BH at q = 0.10 within a batch (or e-LOND online).
- Confirmatory claims: Bonferroni across at most 2-3 hypotheses.
- Hoeffding union bands are kept only as a sanity check (plus or minus 43 points at n=30).

6. MRI, PRECISION, STOPPING.
- Delta_s = 4 Y-points (about 5 Q) for screening; Delta_t = 8 Y-points (about 10 Q) for target replacement claims.
- Planning n/arm = ceil(9.02*sigma_U^2/Delta^2): one-sided alpha 0.10, power 0.8. At sigma 15 this gives 82 for Delta=5 and 21 for Delta=10.
- Pair stopping, leader L vs challenger C. Stop when any of these holds:
  - P(mu_C > mu_L | D) >= 0.95 or <= 0.05;
  - posterior SD(mu_C - mu_L) <= Delta/2 (then decide by posterior mean; ties go to the simpler, cheaper policy);
  - n = n_max (screening 40/arm; target from the budget split).
- Finalist absolute mean: stop at n_t >= 12, when lab SE is at most half the official 3-run SE.
- Below Delta_t, choose by posterior mean, not by significance.

7. ACTIONS.
- REPEAT: some stopping condition is still unmet, or the censoring bounds disagree.
- DORMANT (reversible): n >= n0 and P(mu_p >= mu_L - Delta_s | D) < 0.05. Never decided on partial episodes or on Hoeffding bands.
- RETIRE: only invalid, duplicate-hash or rule-violating artifacts.
- PROMOTE to target: the top 2 by posterior mean with P(best) >= 0.2, if the screening actor holds pruning authority; otherwise the best per family.
- REOPEN: when any of these holds:
  - an audit gives P(mu_t >= mu_t,inc - Delta_t) >= 0.3;
  - a new child hypothesis is proposed;
  - the fair queue reaches it (every dormant family gets at least 1 episode per 5 blocks);
  - the epoch changes (then all cells restart).
- GENERATE: family f may hold ceil((1+N_f)^alpha) evaluated children, where N_f = terminal episodes in its subtree and alpha = beta_hat/(beta_hat+1), with beta_hat = 1 until estimated from child-minus-parent improvements. At least 20% of screening episodes are reserved for generation.
- ALLOCATE among actives: top-two Thompson sampling (beta = 0.5), weighted by cost (proportional to E[T]). Run the knowledge gradient per cost as the alternative arm in the testbed.

8. CALIBRATION AND AUDIT.
- Every target-evaluated policy also gets at least 6 episodes on each screening actor in the same epoch.
- Model: bivariate hierarchical errors-in-variables, (mu_s, mu_t) ~ BVN with measurement variances sigma^2/n. Report the posterior of rho, disattenuated rank correlation, top-k recall, and the regret mu_t(best by cheap) - mu_t(best by target).
- Pruning authority requires all of:
  - K_cal >= 8 shared policies spanning >= 20 Q-points;
  - P(rho > 0.5) >= 0.8;
  - zero audited false rejections.
- Audits:
  - Each dormant candidate is drawn with probability q = 0.2 per block (seeded and logged; at least 1 per two blocks) and run for 3 target episodes.
  - It counts as a false rejection if P(mu_t >= mu_t,inc - Delta_t) >= 0.5.
  - Estimate the false-rejection rate by IPW (weights 1/q) with Clopper-Pearson bounds.
  - One false rejection among the first 5 audits revokes authority for that family or complexity class.

9. SUBMISSION (Stage 1 = max over at most 3 scored versions).
- Submit a distinct valid version at each cutoff: 27 Oct, 30 Oct and 1 Nov, 24:00 GMT.
- Predictive score for version v: m_v = 0.8*mu~_Q + 0.1*D_hat + 0.1*E_hat, with s_v^2 = 0.64(sigma_v^2/3 + v_v) + omega_env^2. omega_env defaults to 5 Stage-1 points until official data arrive.
- Choose argmax EI = (m - A*)Phi(z) + s*phi(z), with z = (m - A*)/s and A* = best issued score.
  - If A* is not yet released, choose by Monte Carlo E[max(A_prev, A_v)].
  - If a public leaderboard shows the top-10 boundary T, maximise P(max(A*, A_v) >= T).
- After each release, compute z_shift = (official - m_v)/s_v. If |z| > 2, raise omega_env and favour policies that are robust across dev conditions.

10. CONFIRMATION.
- Freeze at most 2 finalists plus the incumbent (hashes and protocol id).
- Fixed n_conf per arm: 8 by default, or the section 6 formula with Delta_t if affordable. Run in interleaved blocks with a single look, or at most 3 looks with O'Brien-Fleming z = 3.471, 2.454, 2.004.
- Primary analysis: Welch one-sided 95% lower bound on mu_F - mu_I, Bonferroni alpha/2. Sensitivity: hedged CS on paired differences.
- Confirmation data never feed selection. Any edit after viewing them turns them into development data.
- The dev-environment confirmation does not certify official-environment performance.

11. SPECIALISATION AND LATE BENEFIT.
- Compare complete policies only, intention-to-treat from month 0.
- Calendar rules get a negative-control arm with the switch at M ~ U{5..12}, assigned at launch. If the effect is flat in M, the calendar is not the mechanism.
- Partial-episode proxies are allowed only after validation on completed episodes from at least 10 policies: leave-one-family-out Kendall tau >= 0.7 and no top-3 false rejection.

12. METHOD EVALUATION.
- Replay testbed: a frozen catalog of at least 30 policies with at least 30 episodes each (scripted or cheap actors). Sample without replacement from per-policy outcome pools, with common random numbers across methods. R >= 30 searches per method at equal budget.
- Metrics: simple regret against held-out pool means, P(selected within Delta_s of the best), false-dormancy rate, cost. Compare methods with paired Wilcoxon tests.
- Arms: uniform plus pick-best, successive halving, Best-of-N without feedback, refine-leader, the full method, and ablations (no reopening, archive quota 0/5/10%, no calibration, no diversity, no specialisation).
- Live LLM searches are reported as case studies.

ASSUMPTIONS:
- Fresh episodes are independent and stationary within an epoch, with no cross-session interference through the shared database.
- Y is bounded.
- The normal working model is adequate, as checked by the t and bootstrap refits.
- The dev environment differs from official by a random shift (omega_env).
failure_evidence: Target-pilot SD of Y above 25 points, or a strongly bimodal Y with completion below 30%: Delta_t then needs more than 50 episodes per arm, the target comparison plan is infeasible, and screening should move to completion first.
The hedged confidence sequence and the Bayesian posterior disagree on the sign of a finalist difference, or the Student-t or bootstrap refit flips a decision: the normal working model is inadequate.

The selected policy's confirmation-stage mean falls more than 2 posterior SDs below its exploration-stage posterior mean: tau is overestimated, there is data leakage, or adaptive-sampling bias was not controlled.

There is at least one audited false rejection in the first 5 audits, or the target-best policy falls outside the screening actor's top 3: the cheap actor must lose pruning authority (problem A confirmed).
Recomputing decisions on prefix-complete, launch-ordered data changes them, or Y correlates strongly with wall-clock completion time: asynchrony bias was present.
Censoring exceeds 10% in a cell, or the censoring-rate ratio between compared arms exceeds 2: complete-case estimates are unreliable.
The sentinel incumbent drifts between blocks (CUSUM alarm, or an early-versus-late test at p<0.01), or the route or alias changes: an epoch break that invalidates pooled estimates.
An interim official live-play score falls outside the 95% posterior predictive interval (|z_shift| > 2): the dev-to-official shift dominates and lab precision is no longer the bottleneck.

In the replay testbed, the full method does not beat successive halving or uniform allocation in paired regret at equal budget, or an ablation does as well as the full method: that component adds no value.
A policy in the bottom half on an early (for example month-8) proxy finishes in the top 3 on complete episodes: the proxy is invalid for pruning (problem B confirmed).
Target tokens per month exceed 500k: E varies across policies and the Y' proxy for non-target actors is biased.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. competition-rules.rst.txt L185-198 scores token efficiency per run (tokens/survival_months, cap 50 if the run ends before month 48) and averages it over the three runs. The version score is therefore mean over runs of (0.8Q + 0.1E) + 0.1D, so the per-run objective really is 0.8Q + 0.1E. lab-spec.json L74 and experiment-registry.json (primary_metric 'mean_terminal_quantitative_score' for E01-E03) put Q alone in the decision metric. mathematics.md L9 defines Y = Q/100. The prior documents do know about E: mathematics.md L19 says optimising mu is 'un componente', strategy-dossier.md L21-23 writes out A, and experiment-plan.md L24 lists tokens and survival months for computing efficiency. None of them folds E into the quantity that drives decisions. strategy-dossier.md L37 also discusses survival priority without mentioning the completion cap. The arithmetic checks out: completion versus early exit is worth 0.1 x (100 - 50) = 5 Stage-1 points per run when tokens per month are at most 500k, which is 6.25 Q-points. Y lies in [0,90]. The corrected formula matches the rules.
verdicts.refined_correction: Primary per-episode outcome Y = 0.8Q + 0.1E_run, where E_run = min(cap_T, clip(100(3e6 - tokens/T)/2.5e6, 0, 100)), cap_T = 50 if T<48 and 100 otherwise. 'tokens' is the quantity the official score report calls total_tokens; record it raw, because it is not certain that input+output+cached is the same thing. Y' for non-target actors must not erase token differences between policies: some candidates (for example B3/B5 in experiment-plan.md) exist precisely to change context growth. Use E_hat(C, policy) built from the cheap actor's tokens per month, scaled by a target/cheap token ratio measured on shared policies. Fall back to a constant E_hat(C) only when the target pilot sits well below 500k tokens/month. Severity: moderate to major. The documents acknowledge E but leave it out of decisions.

verdicts.reason: The numbers are verified. With b(n) = sqrt(log(pi^2 n^2/(3 delta))/(2n)) and delta=0.05, the half-widths are 66.3/42.8/25.9 points at n=10/30/100, and 76.8/48.3/28.6 with delta/20. The rule 'upper bound below the other's lower bound' needs a gap of about 2b, roughly 86 points at n=30, so it essentially never fires. I reran widths.py and reproduced the hedged-CS median half-width of 11.2 at n=30, SD 15. The auditor's lambda, the truncation c/m and c/(1-m), the mu_hat/sigma_hat recursions and K± = max{theta K+, (1-theta) K-} all match Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, eq. 24 (ar5iv 2010.09686). The prior text is not mathematically wrong, though. mathematics.md L54 calls it 'una derivación ilustrativa, no la implementación más eficiente' and concedes the bands may eliminate nothing. from-zero-lab.md L77 says 'su rigor no crea información' and 'Es una opción analítica'. The real defect is that this non-operational rule is the only formally specified dormancy criterion. design.md L95 ('evidencia desfavorable') and from-zero-lab.md L73 ('claramente inferiores') leave the working rule undefined.
verdicts.refined_correction: Keep the Hoeffding band only as a labelled worst-case illustration. Define the working dormancy rule separately: a reversible Bayesian posterior rule whose thresholds are calibrated by simulation. Be explicit that even variance-adaptive betting CSs will rarely separate arms at feasible target sample sizes (hedged CS about ±24 points at n=10, ±11 at n=30, SD 15). Anytime-valid claims will therefore mostly be unavailable on the target actor, and they should not gate the ordinary search.

verdicts.reason: The statistical point is correct. If a cell's outcomes are indexed by completion time, the sequence is no longer i.i.d. in index order: short episodes (failures, low Q) arrive first. Interim means and CS evaluated on that sequence are then biased or invalid. Indexing by launch order with prefix-complete data restores validity, and a time-uniform CS stays valid at any random n_c. The citations check out. Nie et al. 2018 show negative bias under adaptive collection. Shin, Ramdas & Rinaldo 2019 show that optimistic sampling gives negative bias, while optimistic stopping and choosing give positive bias; 'either sign' is slightly loose but acceptable. matteo-branch-review.md L21 does report mean survival of 5.9056 months. However, the auditor understates the prior text. mathematics.md L130 already identifies exactly this mechanism, L132 bars pending jobs from estimators, and L134 proposes 'rondas comparables'. The genuine gaps are two: no formal inclusion rule, and the alternative 'decisiones que registren claramente qué resultados faltan' does not remove the bias.
verdicts.refined_correction: Replace the vague alternative in mathematics.md §10 with an explicit rule: estimators and CSs are computed only on launch-indexed, prefix-complete data, or on whole completed rounds. A prefix stalled by a censored launch is resolved by the censoring rule, not by skipping the launch. Severity: moderate. The hazard was identified; only the remedy was underspecified.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed that nothing beyond labelling exists. lab-spec.json L73, mathematics.md L126 and records.schema.json's 'censored' status define no estimator or sensitivity analysis. The reasoning holds. If the interruption hazard is per call, risk grows with episode length. A full run is about 418 MCP calls (budget-and-search.md, 'about 418 MCP calls'), roughly 8x a 6-month failure. Because length correlates with Q, complete-case analysis is biased downward. One part of the auditor's 'correction' already exists: protocol.md §9 L131 says to observe an existing session through the official interface before retrying. What is missing is the resumed flag and any analysis rule.
verdicts.refined_correction: Keep resume-by-observe from protocol.md §9 and add a resumed flag. Note that a resumed LLM episode loses its in-episode memory, so it is a different execution policy. Note too that replacing censored episodes keeps the sample size up but does not remove length-biased selection. Use a tipping-point or delta-adjusted sensitivity analysis as the sensitivity layer, rather than Manski bounds at 0/90. Those bounds have width p_c x 90 (4.5 Y-points at 5% censoring), which does not shrink with n, so 'run another block' can never resolve a flip near Delta_s=4. Treat high or arm-imbalanced censoring as an infrastructure bug to fix before interpreting results.

verdicts.reason: Partly confirmed, and overstated in places. The rules match the auditor: the latest unscored version per cutoff is scored, content-identical versions are not rescored, and Stage 1 is the max (competition-rules.rst.txt L321-344). The arithmetic is correct: 0.8 x 15/sqrt(3) = 6.9, E[max of 2] = +0.564s = +3.9, E[max of 3] = +0.846s = +5.9. The EI values reproduce (2.30 vs 1.15). The official dataset is closed and common to all versions (packages.rst: 'The dataset and parameters used for official evaluation are not published'), so similar policies' scores are positively correlated, and the +3.9/+5.9 figures are upper bounds.

The predictive spread for EI relative to the issued score A* should include only the independent part: the 3-run sampling noise (0.64 sigma_v^2/3), the posterior variance, and any version-specific interaction with the environment. Acknowledge that with a USD 50 target budget these criteria will likely never be met. In that case the cheap actor screens only gross failures (invalid actions, early collapse) and never ranks close contenders.

verdicts.reason: protocol.md already contains the key idea. L152: 'evaluar asignadores sobre un catálogo de políticas congelado permite aislar la selección'. L154 admits that live searches are pilots. What is missing is sizing (number of policies, episodes and replays), not the concept. The auditor's replay testbed also has its own validity problems. R>=30 replays from one frozen catalog are not independent searches: inference is conditional on that catalog and ignores sampling variability between catalogs. Sampling without replacement from 30-episode pools runs out when a method concentrates its budget, and held-out means need episodes kept outside the pools. A flat frozen catalog cannot test components that depend on generation (diversity of proposals, specialisation, reopening through new children), yet the auditor lists those among its ablations.
verdicts.refined_correction: Size the frozen-catalog allocator experiment already proposed in protocol.md L152. Use split pools (search pool versus held-out pool) and resample both policies and episodes, so the variability between catalogs is represented. To ablate reopening and specialisation, pre-generate a lineage tree offline and replay the reveal order. Report live LLM searches as case studies. Get organiser clarification of scale before running hundreds of cheap or scripted episodes (experiment-plan.md L3).

recommendation_objections: The protocol cannot be delivered in the time available. The first cutoff is 27 Oct 24:00 GMT, tomorrow, and that version must be a complete valid final ZIP including presentation.mp4 (submission.rst L113-138). The protocol requires hierarchical Bayesian and errors-in-variables models, hedged CSs, e-processes, e-BH or e-LOND, IPW audits and a replay testbed of 900 or more episodes. Building that would likely use up the competition week. Do the essentials first: the corrected Y, launch-ordered prefix-complete or whole-round data use, resume-or-censor, a posterior-mean choice, and a valid version at each cutoff.

The protocol's budget rules contradict its own requirements. Calibration gets 15% of the target budget N_t, yet pruning authority needs at least 8 shared policies with target episodes (at least 24 target episodes), which is unreachable unless N_t is about 160 or more. The auditor itself estimates 13-110 episodes. Confirmation at Delta_t = 8 Y-points and sigma_Y of about 12 needs 21 per arm, so 42-63 episodes for 2 finalists plus the incumbent, which is more than 30% of any plausible N_t. In practice the protocol mostly falls back to 'estimation' mode, and it should say so up front instead of specifying machinery that will not run.

The Manski-bound rule does not work as written. Bounds at Y = 0 and 90 have width p_c x 90 (4.5 Y-points at 5% censoring), and that width does not shrink with n. So 'record inconclusive and run another block' can never settle a comparison near Delta_s = 4. Same-block replacement keeps the sample size up but does not remove length-biased selection. Prefer resuming the interrupted episode (with a resumed flag) and a tipping-point or delta-adjusted sensitivity analysis.

The e-BH and e-process screening has almost no power at these sample sizes. With Z = (Y_A - Y_B + 90)/180, a 4-Y-point excess over Delta moves E[Z] by only about 0.022, while SD(Z) is about 0.094. The best log-wealth growth is then about 0.027 per pair, so W is about 3 after 40 pairs, against a required 20 for a single test and K/(qk) = 200 for K=20, k=1 at q=0.10. Screening is an allocation problem; casting it as FDR-controlled testing adds complexity and will reject nothing.

Confirming against the incumbent does not affect Stage-1 decisions. Stage 1 is a max, and a lower later score cannot reduce it, so the choice at each cutoff is among unscored candidates. The incumbent's official score is already known. Spending 30% of target episodes on Welch or O'Brien-Fleming confirmation serves the expert-review story, not the score. A cheaper use of the incumbent is as a sentinel that calibrates the dev-to-official shift.

The EI submission rule puts omega_env in the incremental predictive SD. The evaluation dataset is closed and common to all versions, so most of the dev-to-official shift is shared and already reflected in A*. Counting it again inflates EI and pushes the choice toward high-variance policies. The E[max] gains (+3.9/+5.9) assume independent version scores and are upper bounds. Seeking variance also sits uneasily with the official advice to 'design for consistent performance across repeated runs' and with the robustness criteria in Stage 2 review. Which version's design docs get reviewed is still unresolved (strategy-dossier.md L213).

The non-target proxy Y' = 0.8Q + 0.1 E_hat(C) treats token efficiency as the same for every policy. That erases exactly the differences that token-focused candidates (experiment-plan B3/B5) are meant to change. Token use per month should be measured per policy and mapped to target-equivalent tokens through a ratio calibrated on shared policies.

The replay testbed's conclusions only hold for the one catalog it was built from, and it cannot test components that depend on generation (diversity, specialisation, reopening through new children). Building 30 or more policies with 30 or more episodes each, plus live scripted searches, is unusual scale, and experiment-plan.md L3 and the organiser-question process say such scale must be cleared with the organisers first.

The randomized switch-month negative control is fine inside the lab. Its write-up should state that any month threshold fitted on dev data must not be shipped in a Skill, because the rules prohibit unpublished thresholds presented as rules. Only publicly documented calendar structure, such as the semiannual reviews, may appear in a submission.

audit.dimension: Search and generation methods: tree and evolutionary LLM search, candidate generation, allocation of evaluations, and selection under stochastic, expensive, actor-dependent episodes
audit.verdict_summary: Most citations hold up. Every arXiv ID, title and author list I checked matches its primary record: MCTS-AHD, AB-MCTS, ShinkaEvolve, AdaEvolve, GEPA, EvoTest, ReEvo, TreeFlex, TreeSeeker, Meta-TTL, PACEvolve++ and Empirical-MCTS. The FunSearch ID correction is right, and the Unagi and AHC058 figures match the authors' own reports. The research also gets several hard points right: max-backup and noisy-max selection bias, the positive-part improvement bias, separating "replicate" from "refine/generate", treating a policy's own value separately from its family's potential, using whole episodes as the resource rather than truncated months, and never counting pending jobs as observations. The core weakness is which literature carries the weight. Every flagship precedent (MCTS-AHD, AB-MCTS, ShinkaEvolve, AdaEvolve, GEPA, FunSearch) scores each candidate once with a deterministic or surrogate evaluator, so they inform only the cheap part of our problem, proposing candidates. AB-MCTS's own results show plain repeated sampling (best-of-N) matching or beating it at its main budget, which the research does not mention. The fields built for our expensive part, choosing among stochastic configurations with repeated looks, are absent: algorithm configuration (F-Race/irace, ParamILS, SMAC), ranking-and-selection, practical best-arm identification (LUCB, successive halving/rejects), noisy evolutionary strategies, the optimizer's curse, and infinitely-many-armed bandits. Racing, irace, SMAC, ParamILS and LUCB appear nowhere in the research; Track-and-Stop appears only, unselected, in the search log. The one concrete statistical rule proposed (Hoeffding plus union-bound dormancy) cannot eliminate anything at feasible sample sizes. The selection objective is also misstated: it ignores the token-efficiency term and the rule that Stage 1 takes the best of up to three released versions. There are several misreadings (AHC058, ShinkaEvolve ablations, HOO/StoSOO structure, AdaEvolve "theory"), and the six-milestone plan does not match the release cutoffs on 27 Oct, 30 Oct and 1 Nov. My recommendation is to keep LLM trace-based generation as the proposer, but run it under a release-aligned racing procedure. That procedure re-evaluates the incumbent every round, uses variance-adaptive soft elimination, audits the cheap tier on the target model, confirms candidates on fresh data after freezing, and is compared at equal budget against best-of-N, always-refine-leader and plain racing.

errors.claim: Conservative dormancy rule: retire a fixed policy when its Hoeffding + union-bound upper band b_i(n)=sqrt(log(pi^2 n^2/(3 delta_i))/(2n)) falls below a contender's lower band.
errors.problem: The rule is inoperative at any feasible sample size. On the 0-100 scale with delta=0.05, the half-width for the first candidate is ±68 at n=10, ±44 at n=30 and ±26 at n=100; the 10th candidate gets ±83, ±52 and ±30. The from-zero-lab K-version with K=4 gives ±71 at n=10 and ±45 at n=30. Two bands separate only when the true gap exceeds about twice the half-width, so with tens of episodes per candidate nothing is ever retired, and allocation silently becomes uniform. The cause is the range-based bound: it assumes a worst-case standard deviation of 50 points, whereas policy-level SDs are plausibly 10-20. The text concedes the bands 'pueden ser tan anchas', yet keeps the rule as the dormancy criterion.
errors.correction: Use variance-adaptive procedures. Options: fully sequential indifference-zone ranking and selection (Kim-Nelson 'KN': unknown, unequal variances, eliminate when inferiority is clear); empirical-Bernstein or betting confidence sequences for anytime-valid monitoring; or a Normal-Inverse-Gamma posterior with soft elimination when P(mu_i > mu_leader) < 0.10. Dormancy is reversible, so loose error control is acceptable while searching. Keep strict control only for the frozen, fresh confirmation, and state the resolution limit openly: at sigma=15, detecting a 5-point difference needs about 142 episodes per arm, and a 10-point difference about 36.
evidence: Own computation from the formulas in mathematics.md §4 and from-zero-lab.md §5A (values above)
Waudby-Smith & Ramdas (2024) JRSS-B, Estimating means of bounded random variables by betting, https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssb/qkad009

errors.claim: MCTS-AHD is the 'precedente más directo' and 'closely matches the proposed outer policy tree'; use an approach inspired by MCTS-AHD/AB-MCTS to decide where to generate variants.
errors.problem: Both papers score each node once, with deterministic or surrogate evaluators. MCTS-AHD scores a heuristic on fixed instance sets (for example 64 TSP50 instances), with T=1,000 evaluations and max backup. Its ablation gaps are about 0.3-1.5 percentage points from 5 runs, with no SDs in the main text. AB-MCTS states that it 'assumes the existence of a reliable score evaluator', uses a 2^7=128-call budget, and has no replicate action; its Bayesian posterior models variation among newly generated children, not measurement noise of a fixed node. Its own Table 1 shows repeated sampling (best-of-N) beating AB-MCTS-M on ARC-AGI at 128 calls (15.0 vs 12.3 with GPT-4o; 18.6 vs 16.0 with DeepSeek-V3), and on LiveCodeBench the gap is within error bars. So the 'most direct precedent' covers only the cheap part of our problem (proposals) and none of the expensive part (replicated stochastic evaluation).
errors.correction: Present MCTS-AHD and AB-MCTS as generation-side inspiration only: retaining weak candidates, progressive widening, and an explicit generate-vs-refine choice. Base the allocation of evaluations on algorithm configuration, ranking-and-selection and best-arm identification. Make best-of-N (repeated sampling from the seed prompt) a first-class equal-budget baseline. Protocol §10 already lists it; actually run it.
evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2501.08603v3 (Eq. 5, max backup, PW floor(N^0.5)>=|children|, T=1000, Table 5 ablations)
https://arxiv.org/html/2503.04412v5 (Table 1 results; limitation 'assumes the existence of a reliable score evaluator')

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/bibliography.md (55 sources); design.md; mathematics.md; protocol.md; completion-audit.md row 1
errors.claim: The selected sources identify the mathematical methods that fit the proposed tree and allocation problem.
errors.problem: A grep of research/*.md and research/hierarchical-lab/* finds no mention of racing, F-Race, irace, ParamILS, SMAC, LUCB or successive halving/rejects. Track-and-Stop occurs only in search-audit.json, as an unselected candidate. These fields exist precisely to choose among stochastic configurations that are expensive to evaluate, under repeated looks: iterated racing with elitism, incumbent intensification (a challenger may displace the incumbent only after matching its number of runs), indifference-zone ranking and selection, and noisy evolutionary computation (parent re-evaluation, resampling). The section 'Fundamentos... estadística' contains only top-two best-arm identification, confidence sequences, Hyperband/ASHA/BOHB and multi-fidelity Bayesian optimisation.

errors.claim: The estimand is mu = E[quantitative_score/100], and the selection objective is the simple regret of a single returned policy.
errors.problem: (a) The automated version score is 0.8*mean Q + 0.1*D + 0.1*TE. TE is computed per run and capped at 50 when a run ends before month 48, so at equal Q a completed run can be worth up to 5 more automated points than an early exit. (b) Stage 1 is the highest valid version score over the two interim releases and the final release, with one scored version per cutoff, and a lower later score does not reduce it. The decision is therefore a portfolio/top-m problem with an option payoff E[max(S_banked, S_new)], not single-arm simple regret. Once a score is banked, a lower confidence threshold for promotion is rational, and having distinct strong candidates for R2 and R3 has value.
errors.correction: Use a per-run primary estimand A = 0.8*Q + 0.1*TE_run, plus 0.1*D estimated per version, and keep Q as an auxiliary. At each release, choose the distinct candidate that maximises the Monte Carlo value of E[max(S_banked, S_new)]. Model S_new as 0.8 x the mean of 3 posterior-predictive draws plus the TE and D terms. Target top-m identification, with m equal to the remaining releases, which is what LUCB and top-two methods do. Expert-review version coherence remains an open organiser question (organiser-questions.md Q8).

errors.claim: ShinkaEvolve's ablations favour preserving diversity over always climbing from the leader.
errors.problem: The ablations were run only on circle packing (Fig. 9 caption: 'Method Ablation Studies on Circle Packing'), a deterministic geometric evaluator; seed counts and error bars are not stated. The paper itself says 'Hill climbing shows strong initial performance but plateaus quickly.' At this week's budget (tens of candidates, each needing several noisy episodes) we are in the early regime, where the cited evidence favours greedy refinement. GEPA's ablation (Pareto 61.28 vs SelectBestCandidate 54.89 aggregate, Qwen3-8B) is better evidence for frontier-based parent selection, but it depends on shared task instances.
errors.correction: Treat the diversity, archive and reopening machinery as an ablation hypothesis, not a premise. Use always-refine-leader with parent re-evaluation as the main baseline. Keep only a minimal archive (for example 3 families) and a reopening quota as cheap toggles.
evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.19349v1 (parent-selection ablation, Fig. 9 on circle packing; 'Hill climbing shows strong initial performance but plateaus quickly')

errors.claim: AHC058 shows that a mutation which changes the approach can be worth more than many minimal variations: 'Diverse construction and structural mutations can outperform narrow local tweaks'.
errors.problem: This is a category error. The 'large-scale' moves are simulated-annealing neighbourhood operators inside the submitted contest program ('three types of operations for large-scale plan changes using Greedy methods'), not mutations that the agent's search applied. Sakana states that identifying which agent design elements mattered most 'remains an important research task'.
errors.correction: Cite AHC058 only for scale (about USD 1,300; 2,654 GPT-5.2 calls and 2,119 Gemini 3 Pro calls) and for its fast local evaluator. Drop the inference about operators.

errors.location: research/from-zero-lab.md §7 ('la mejor inspiración inmediata'); bibliography.md R05 (scope: abstract_and_verified_metadata); experiment-plan.md §7; strategy-dossier.md §12
errors.claim: GEPA (trace reflection plus a candidate frontier) is the best immediate inspiration.
errors.problem: The research rests its strongest recommendation on a paper it read only at abstract level. GEPA's frontier is a per-instance Pareto front over D_pareto, so it needs shared, repeatable task instances; CareerSim has no seed or instance identity, so that front has nothing to index. GEPA also accepts a mutant if its average improves on one minibatch, which under episode-level noise is a single-draw winner's-curse filter. The main benchmarks report no repeated evaluation or seeds.
errors.correction: Borrow trace diagnosis aggregated over at least 3 episodes and parent sampling weighted by posterior, not by argmax. Replace minibatch acceptance with racing. Any substitute notion of 'instance' (for example situation types) must avoid tuning to specific events.
evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.19457v2 (Algorithm 1 minibatch acceptance; Pareto over training instances)

errors.claim: HOO/StoSOO/BAST provide theory under structure and regularity; the gap is that prompt similarity has not been shown to bound descendants.
errors.problem: HOO and StoSOO build nested partitions of a fixed metric domain: a child is a sub-cell of its parent's cell, and StoSOO samples each node k times before expanding it. A lineage tree of LLM-generated policies is not a partition, because descendants are new points not contained in the parent. The mismatch is structural, not just unproven smoothness. BAST, which was published at UAI 2007 but is listed as a tech report, assumes a fixed finite tree.
errors.correction: State plainly that these methods do not apply. For 'draw a new candidate vs re-sample an existing one', cite infinitely-many-armed bandits: Wang, Audibert & Munos 2008 set K ∝ n^{β/(1+β)}, which is √n for β=1 and matches MCTS-AHD's α=0.5 progressive widening; Carpentier & Valko 2015 cover simple regret.

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/findings.md ('Its theory and results...'); README.md table ('Repartir trabajadores según progreso | AdaEvolve')
errors.claim: AdaEvolve's theory and results do not transfer automatically; AdaEvolve is the method for allocating workers by progress.
errors.problem: AdaEvolve makes no formal theoretical claims. Its signal δ=max((f'−f*)/f*,0), accumulated as G_t=ρG_{t−1}+(1−ρ)δ², uses single evaluations; no repeated evaluation is reported. That is exactly the selection-biased statistic mathematics.md §8 warns about, but the research never names AdaEvolve as its source. AdaEvolve's UCB allocates LLM generation budget across islands, not evaluation replicates. Its ablations use 3 runs on 2 tasks.
errors.correction: Name AdaEvolve and ShinkaEvolve (bandit reward exp(max(r−r_b,0))−1) as concrete sources of positive-part noise bias. Use posterior-confirmed improvement as the productivity and stagnation signal.
evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.20133v1 (improvement signal, UCB C=√2, Table 4 ablations ±std over 3 runs)

errors.claim: EvoTest: an actor/evolver loop that revises configuration between game episodes.
errors.problem: The description is accurate but misses EvoTest's most transferable mechanism. EvoTest runs UCB over the parent plus m children, scores each configuration by whole single episodes, and keeps the parent as a fallback. Without UCB, Detective AUC drops from 0.94 to 0.68, and evolver strength matters (Qwen3-8B 0.68 vs o3 0.94). Its objective is AUC over K=50 consecutive episodes in deterministic-reset Jericho games, a cumulative objective rather than simple regret.
errors.correction: Cite EvoTest as the closest precedent for noisy one-episode evaluation of evolved configurations. Note that its objective differs and that its state-action memory tables are prohibited here.

errors.claim: Run 100 sessions of one candidate, or screen four candidates with 2 games each and then take the top 2.
errors.problem: Both are fixed N chosen without reference to observed variability. A hundred target runs on one untested candidate yield precision on one arm and no selection information. With 2 games per candidate at σ≈15, each mean has SE≈10.6, so the top-2 pick is near-random unless gaps exceed about 20 points.
errors.correction: Use sequential racing with a first stage of n0=3-4, then top-two or LUCB allocation, stopping on the posterior criterion and the budget.

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/protocol.md §5 (calibration pilot 6 policies x 2 actors x 3 episodes)
errors.claim: A 36-episode fidelity matrix comes before the cheap actor may eliminate directions.
errors.problem: There is no pre-registered rule for when the cheap tier gains or loses pruning power. With 3 episodes per cell, the SE per cell is about σ/√3 ≈ 8.7, so a 6-item rank correlation is dominated by noise unless the true gaps exceed about 15 points. The matrix also confounds model with harness: Claude Code CLI with MCP for the cheap worker versus JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 for the target.
errors.correction: Embed the calibration into the race as an audit stream: each round, send 1 randomly chosen cheap-rejected candidate to the target model. Add an explicit revocation rule, keep the harness as close as possible to JiuwenSwarm (same SKILL.md files and manifest instruction), and label the actor as a model+harness pair.
evidence: https://proceedings.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/71c31ebf577ffdad5f4a74156daad518-Paper-Conference.pdf (multi-fidelity BAI assumes a known bias bound on the cheap source)

confirmed.claim: MCTS-AHD: Zheng, Xie, Wang, Hooi; ICML 2025 (PMLR 267); arXiv 2501.08603. It keeps all heuristics in a tree, uses max-child backup and progressive widening (floor(N^0.5) ≥ |children|), and lets temporarily weak heuristics be developed further.
confirmed.evidence: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/zheng25o.html; https://arxiv.org/html/2501.08603v3

confirmed.claim: AB-MCTS: arXiv 2503.04412, NeurIPS 2025 spotlight. A GEN node chooses wider vs deeper by Thompson sampling, with mixed-model and node-aggregation Bayesian variants.
confirmed.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2503.04412v5 (author comment: spotlight at NeurIPS 2025)

confirmed.claim: ShinkaEvolve: Lange, Imajuku, Cetin; arXiv 2509.19349; ICLR 2026. It uses archive and islands, novelty rejection (embedding cosine similarity >0.95, then an LLM judge) and UCB1 selection over the LLM ensemble.
confirmed.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.19349v1; https://iclr.cc/virtual/2026/poster/10007692

confirmed.claim: AdaEvolve: arXiv 2602.20133, Cemri et al. 2026 preprint. It has three levels: local exploration intensity, bandit allocation across islands, and meta-guidance on stagnation.
confirmed.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20133; https://arxiv.org/html/2602.20133v1

confirmed.claim: Copying max backup onto noisy episode scores amplifies selection bias, so a policy's own estimate must be kept separate from its family's potential (mathematics.md §2-3).
confirmed.evidence: MCTS-AHD assumes deterministic evaluation on a fixed instance set (https://arxiv.org/html/2501.08603v3); the logic follows the optimizer's curse (Smith & Winkler 2006, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.1050.0451)

confirmed.claim: A positive-part improvement signal is biased upward under noise (mathematics.md §8).
confirmed.evidence: This is exactly AdaEvolve's δ=max((f'−f*)/f*,0) and ShinkaEvolve's exp(max(r−r_b,0))−1 reward, both computed on single evaluations (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.20133v1; https://arxiv.org/html/2509.19349v1)

confirmed.claim: The venue and metadata for GEPA (ICLR 2026 oral), EvoTest (ICLR 2026), ReEvo (NeurIPS 2024), Meta-TTL v4, PACEvolve++ v2 and Empirical-MCTS are accurate.
