Overstatements: (a) protocol.md section 3 explicitly says the 1M/100k figures are illustrative, unmeasured, and that retained history changes consumption and price tier. (b) 'Not addressed beyond pending is not zero' is wrong: mathematics.md section 10 discusses time-to-result selection (bad games finish first), protocol.md section 9 records an operational cause, and the schema has status censored/infrastructure_failure plus termination_reason. The order of magnitude is plausible. Matteo's random baseline gives 1,563,578 actions / 73,858 sessions over 5.9 months, about 3.6 take_action calls per month, or about 173 per 48 months and 350+ turns. Retained history then implies 10^7-10^8 cumulative input tokens, and the full-score efficiency bound is 24M per 48-month run.
verdicts.refined_correction: Express Claude cost as measured subscription usage per episode: stream-json rate_limit events, total_cost_usd as an API-equivalent figure, and wall-clock. Add a subscription unit to the schema. On a rate-limit stop, wait for the window to reset and resume the same conversation instead of burning continuations. Record interruption_cause from the stream (rate_limit, timeout, context_reset, crash). Compare interruption rates by survival month. An HTTP transport is not required for resumption, because the per-episode DB persists and a new stdio server can observe the session, as careerlab's verifier already does. Replace the 1M illustration with pilot measurements.

verdicts.reason: Partly confirmed. design.md line 140, lab-spec sample_cheap_rejections_on_target and protocol section 11 give no audit size, inclusion probability, estimand, threshold or revocation rule. The SE arithmetic is right: sigma/sqrt(3) is about 8.7-11.5 for sigma 15-20. One part is refuted: mathematics.md line 106 specifies 'auditoría aleatoria de rechazadas', a random audit, so the claim that the rate is 'biased by whichever candidates the orchestrator chose' does not apply to the prior as written. Under uniform random audits the simple mean is already unbiased. Horvitz-Thompson weighting is needed only if the auditor's non-uniform probabilities are adopted. Revocation is mentioned vaguely in mathematics.md line 110 but not operationalised.
verdicts.refined_correction: Pre-register the audit: random selection with logged probabilities (uniform is acceptable; non-uniform needs HT weights), episodes per audit, the pooled estimands (mean target gap and calibration z-scores against the predictive interval), and revocation thresholds that re-queue every cheap-pruned candidate in the stratum. State openly that single-candidate significance tests with 2 episodes have almost no power; revocation will in practice rest on the pooled calibration and exceedance checks.

verdicts.reason: Refuted as stated. The auditor says the prior 'assumes Claude workers are weaker executors than deepseek-v4-flash'. design.md line 136 only says a complex policy 'puede fallar con Haiku por ejecución', which is a possibility, not a ranking against the target. The prior also already restricts Sonnet to a separate, diagnostic condition. protocol.md section 5 item 2 says to add Sonnet 'para estudiar ejecución cuando haya una razón concreta'. lab-spec alternate_actor says 'Separate actor condition', and design.md line 148 forbids pooling or treating it as the official runtime. Nothing in the prior uses Sonnet scores to promote a policy. The alternative risk the auditor raises (stronger actors filling gaps in a Skill) is an untested hypothesis, and its evidence cuts both ways: Sclar et al. show weak cross-model correlation, while ADAS reports transfer. The useful additions are new content rather than corrections of an error: target-model comprehension probes and the s_b,C/s_b,T compression check.
verdicts.refined_correction: No error to correct. Optionally make explicit in design.md section 13 that a Sonnet arm answers only the diagnostic question 'is the procedure bad, or did the executor fail?' and never feeds promotion. Add cheap target-model comprehension probes and a compression-ratio check as covariates.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. In records.schema.json, evaluation (lines 172-216) and job (lines 401-431) both have additionalProperties:false and carry only actor_model_id as a string. execution_class has only development_non_target, target_platform_representative and synthetic_fixture. The cost object supports only USD. There are mitigations: epoch_id can encode the environment or split, protocol.md line 120 hashes the artifact 'incluida la configuración relevante del prompt', and careerlab writes actor.json and a server fingerprint (model, effort, skills_mode, autocompact, cli_version, split, competition_mode) outside the schema. So the information is partly captured in code but cannot be validated by the record contract. Severity is moderate rather than major.
verdicts.refined_correction: Add an actor_config object (or a reference with its hash) aligned with careerlab's actor.json and fingerprint() fields: route, key_class, served model, provider log reference, harness and version, system_prompt_sha256, skill_loading, effort, context policy, mcp_server_cmd_sha256, competition_mode, split. Also add a compliance block, an interruption_cause enum, a subscription-usage cost unit, and an official_evaluation class or a separate record type for the 3 official runs.

recommendation_objections: The cheap-actor pruning license (L1) cannot realistically be reached under the auditor's own parameters. With s_b=5 and sigma=15, n* = ceil(2.33*9) = 21, far above the 'n* <= 4' top-up condition. With K=10, even a perfectly measured r=0.8 gives an 80% lower bound of only about 0.55 against the 'rho_true >= 0.5' criterion, and noisy n=2 cells widen it further. The protocol would therefore spend about 40 matrix episodes plus about 1,200 replay calls to almost certainly conclude 'no pruning' (L0). Pre-compute the probability of reaching L1. If it is low, drop the calibration matrix and use target-only selection, with Claude cells kept for queue ordering and diagnosis.

The auditor ignored the untracked careerlab/ harness, written today. careerlab/actors/claude_cli.py already uses --setting-sources '', --strict-mcp-config, --tools '', game-only --allowedTools, --system-prompt, stream-json and a per-episode --competition server, with run directories outside the repo. Recommendation 2 should read 'document, attest and validate' rather than 'build'. Its suggestion of --safe-mode is risky: the CLI help lists MCP servers among the customizations safe mode disables, so it may break --mcp-config. Test it first. --system-prompt also does not remove CLAUDE.md or memory context; verify their absence separately, for example with a clean CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR.

Decision-level replay is not 'cheap (one call per decision)'. Each replayed context can reach 10^5 tokens or more, so 600-1,200 replays on the target could consume a large share of the USD 50 key. It is also unverified that exact JiuwenSwarm contexts can be extracted, and calling the competition key from a custom replay script may be contested as an 'unrelated application'. Measure context size in the pilot and ask the organisers, or use the team-funded route. One-step agreement conditional on the target's own history also does not capture compounding differences, so the PDI threshold of 0.15 has no grounding.

TOST equivalence within +/-3 points is infeasible at sigma of about 15 with plausible n; it needs on the order of a hundred or more episodes per arm. The A1/A2 pooling criterion (ii) is therefore decorative and will always fail. Either pool by design (same slug and harness, provider logged, route as a random effect) or keep A2 separate, but do not pre-register a test that cannot pass. Similarly, the Holm-adjusted 'audited candidate beats the incumbent by more than Delta_min' revocation test has almost no power with 2 episodes per audit.

OpenRouter default routing on a team key is price-weighted, so it will oversample the cheapest providers, including fp4 Relace. Organiser routing 'is set by the organisers' and may be pinned. 'Default routing' therefore does not make A2 near-gold: log the provider and model the route effect instead of assuming equivalence.

The interruption recommendation should address a concrete failure in the existing code. After any stop, careerlab re-prompts up to 3 times as fresh processes (--no-session-persistence). A rate-limit stop burns all three continuations immediately and is recorded as 'not finished after 3 continuations', and every continuation is a context reset concentrated in long episodes, confounded with problem B. The fix is to wait for the usage window to reset, resume the same conversation, and label context-reset continuations as a distinct actor configuration. HTTP transport is not needed for resumption, because the per-episode DB persists and a new stdio server can observe the session.

Schedule and budget realism are not addressed. Six days remain, and the first cutoff is 24:00 on 27 Oct. The protocol calls for a pilot, 40 matrix episodes, top-ups, audits and 8-10 frozen confirmation episodes per finalist on A1. Target episodes may take 30-120 minutes and an unknown $1-10 each, and concurrency is not yet authorised. The plan needs a time-boxed minimal version. The 'reserve at least 40% of the key for confirmation' rule should also be weighed against Stage 1 being the maximum over at most three scored versions, where a weaker later version does not lower the score.

Several literature citations are stretched. Dorner et al. bound LLM-judge labelling of the same items, so the result is an analogy here, not a bound on cheap actors. Kennedy-O'Hagan co-kriging is the policy-level calibration model the prior already proposed, not an inapplicable method. The S2LPP re-annotation (recommendation 16) is barely needed: bibliography.md R43 already limits it to QA/NLI, and the abstract I fetched reports positive transfer, with no 'mixed results' or GPT-3.5 target stated there.

The Opus checklist judge needs 50 hand-labelled decisions at accuracy of at least 0.85. That human labelling during competition week is not budgeted. Use automated, rule-checkable compliance metrics first (invalid or unaffordable attempts, blind retries, missing notes) and add the judge only if time allows.

audit.dimension: Problem B: late benefits (partial-episode screening, surrogate endpoints, survival/censoring of early exits, delayed credit assignment)
audit.verdict_summary: The research gets the headline right and says it consistently. It says to run complete episodes, not to cut at month 8 or 12, to score early exits rather than drop them, never to impute a score for an interrupted run, and never to count pending jobs as zero. It also decomposes survivor-conditioning bias correctly (mathematics.md §12, counterexamples.json). But it stops at prohibitions. There is no procedure that could ever license partial-episode screening, or show it is invalid. There is no survival or censoring estimator, the records contract stores no per-month trajectory, and the audit design does not target late-benefit false rejections. The primary outcome (mean quantitative_score) leaves out the token-efficiency term. That term is itself a late-benefit term: a run ending before month 48 is capped at 50, and tokens per month can grow with survival. Censoring and asynchrony are correctly named, but the implied handling (complete-case means, decisions taken asynchronously) is biased against long-surviving policies, which are the ones problem B is about. The example allocation in experiment-plan.md (4 candidates × 2 games, keep the top 2) is a rank-based successive-halving cut on two noisy episodes, so the same late-benefit failure reappears in sample space. The literature on this dimension is cited at abstract level (Hyperband/ASHA/BOHB). It misses the most direct primary evidence: Hyperband's own hedge bracket and stated failure case, the slow-start failures of freeze-thaw and learning-curve extrapolation, short-horizon bias, and the clinical toolkit of surrogate validation, short-term-endpoint seamless designs, delayed-response group-sequential tests, RMST, competing risks and IPCW. Recommendation: no truncation of running LLM episodes this week; use partial information only to set launch priority; log full trajectories so a shadow surrogate analysis can be reported; handle censoring explicitly; audit dormant candidates at random; and pre-register a screening gate that, by its own numbers, is unlikely to open on the target actor before 1 Nov.

errors.claim: The primary outcome is the mean terminal quantitative_score under the target actor.
errors.problem: This leaves out the part of the official per-run score that depends on survival. TE is computed from total_tokens / survival_months and is capped at 50 for any run ending before month 48. Reaching month 48 is therefore worth up to 0.1 x 50 = 5 automated points (6.25 quantitative_score points) beyond Q. A Q-only metric undervalues late-benefit policies that complete the run. It also overvalues long-surviving, token-hungry policies whose tokens per month rise with episode length. budget-and-search.md §3 has the correct formula, but it never reaches the lab spec or the registry.
errors.correction: Primary per-run outcome on the target runtime: U = 0.8*Q + 0.1*TE. TE uses the published formula, with the 50 cap when months < 48 and 0 when the token or month count is missing. The policy estimand is mu_U(policy, target, epoch). Report Q, months survived, P(T=48) and tokens/month as separate auxiliaries. For non-target actors, report Q and survival only and mark TE as not comparable across actors.
evidence: competition-rules.rst.txt, Token efficiency score (10%): tokens_per_month = total_tokens / survival_months; a run that ends before month 48 is capped at 50
research/budget-and-search.md §3 (correct TE arithmetic: 24M and 144M boundaries, 80 at 1M tokens/month)

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/records.schema.json $defs.evaluation (terminal-only fields, additionalProperties:false) vs research/experiment-plan.md §2 lines 23 and 28 and research/from-zero-lab.md §9 line 159
errors.claim: The five record types are the contract for what the lab persists.
errors.problem: The evaluation record holds only terminal fields: terminal_score, survival_months, full_horizon_completion and a free-text termination_reason. It has no per-month trajectory of visible stats, level, CurrentLevelDuration, review grades, promotions, warnings, quarterly allocations or cumulative tokens. It also lacks ending-dimension contributions, a censoring month and a resumed flag. This contradicts the plan's own metric lists (review outcomes, ending contributions, per-transition logging). With additionalProperties:false, these fields cannot even be added ad hoc. Without them, late benefits cannot be detected and no month-k surrogate can be validated after the fact.
errors.correction: Add a 'trajectory' record type with one row per month boundary plus one per review and quarterly phase. Add terminal fields: ending_contributions, termination_category (enum), censor_month, resumed (bool) and tokens_cumulative_by_month. See the protocol.

errors.claim: An administrative interruption is censored, not scored; incomplete episodes are recorded rather than imputed.
errors.problem: The label is right, but no estimator is specified, so the default becomes a complete-case mean. That is biased whenever interruption risk grows with episode length. Long episodes make more tool calls, run longer and are more exposed to rate limits, timeouts, context overflow and contention on the shared career_emulator.sqlite3. They are removed disproportionately, which pulls down the estimate for exactly the long-surviving, late-benefit policies. Replacing an interrupted episode with a fresh one does not remove this length-biased selection.
errors.correction: (a) Resume rather than censor: re-attach to the same session_id through observe/check_latest_logs (or the runner's --continue for the target), and set resumed=true. (b) Estimate survival with Kaplan-Meier, and cause-specific cumulative incidence with Aalen-Johansen, under censoring. (c) Estimate the mean of the end-of-episode quantity U by IPCW, weighting complete episodes by 1/G_hat(T), where G_hat is the KM of the censoring time in months (Bang & Tsiatis 2000). (d) Report best- and worst-case bounds. (e) Freeze decisions if more than 10% of a policy's episodes are censored, or if the censoring rate rises with month.
evidence: Bang & Tsiatis 2000, Biometrika 87(2):329-343, doi:10.1093/biomet/87.2.329: IPCW mean of an end-of-follow-up quantity under censoring
quickstart.rst.txt: runner writes a shared state database career_emulator.sqlite3

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/mathematics.md §10 (lines 128-134); protocol.md §6 ('El planificador puede ser asíncrono')
errors.claim: Pending jobs are not observations; the first version should use comparable rounds or decisions that record which results are missing.
errors.problem: The diagnosis is correct but the remedy is optional. In asynchronous operation the first results to arrive are early exits, so a policy's interim mean is pessimistic precisely when its good episodes are long. An ASHA-style promotion or a dormancy decision taken on interim results is a hidden partial-episode screen. The clinical literature handles these 'pipeline' units explicitly (Hampson & Jennison 2013), and the research does not adopt that.
errors.correction: Make it binding: dormancy or rejection of a policy only at round close, when every episode launched for it in that round is terminal or properly handled as censored. Use interim data only for launch priority. In interim displays, show pending episodes as right-censored at their current month (KM), never as zeros and never as missing.
evidence: Hampson & Jennison 2013, JRSS-B 75(1):3-54 (group sequential tests with delayed responses/pipeline subjects)
mathematics.md §10 itself notes bad episodes finish faster

errors.claim: Illustrative allocation: four candidates with two complete games each, then the strongest two get five more.
errors.problem: This is successive halving with r=2 episodes and a rank cut. It has no interval criterion and no audit of the candidates it drops. Outcomes are bimodal (early exit vs completion), so pairwise misranking at n=2 is Phi(-Delta/(sigma*sqrt(2/n))), about 37% for Delta=5 and sigma=15 and about 25% for Delta=10. Late-benefit policies, such as those investing early in Skill or risk defusal, tend to be the high-variance ones, so they are cut more often.
errors.correction: Cut only on pre-registered interval or posterior criteria. Send cut candidates to dormancy with randomized audits. If staging is kept, hedge with a no-cut lane of at least 30% of the budget (the analogue of Hyperband's s=0 bracket).
evidence: Li et al. 2018 Hyperband JMLR 18: §3.2 bracket s=0 performs classical random search with full resource; §4.4.3 failure case when small-resource performance is not indicative
Normal-approximation misranking arithmetic (illustrative sigma; replace with observed sigma)

errors.claim: Hyperband, ASHA and BOHB are useful; the number of complete episodes is a more defensible resource than truncation.
errors.problem: The direction is right, but the justification is thin and partly misleading. (i) Hyperband's analysis treats each arm's loss sequence as deterministic with converging limits (§5.2). With episodes as the resource, the rung statistic is a noisy sample mean, so successive-halving guarantees do not carry over; this is racing or best-arm-identification territory. (ii) The paper's own robustness mechanism, hedging across brackets including full-resource s=0, is not mentioned. (iii) The literature that directly documents problem B is missing. Freeze-thaw BO assumes curves decay exponentially toward an asymptote. Domhan-style and LC-PFN extrapolation use increasing-trend priors, and LC-PFN reports that every termination criterion it tested failed on curves with an inflection point. Short-horizon bias (Wu et al. 2018) shows short-horizon objectives systematically pick the wrong long-horizon setting.
errors.correction: Cite these and state the consequence: curve-extrapolation priors are structurally wrong for career trajectories. These trajectories are non-monotone, change regime at the 6-month review and promotion windows, and are absorbed by death. For the episode-count resource, use racing/BAI with intervals plus a hedge lane.
evidence: Adriaensen et al. NeurIPS 2023 arXiv:2310.20447 §3.2, §4.3, §5 (increasing-curve filter; failure on inflection curves; 'slow start' not modelled)
Wu, Ren, Liao, Grosse ICLR 2018 arXiv:1803.02021

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/mathematics.md §9 para 2; design.md §8 table row line 102; counterexamples.json 'early_proxy_reversal'
errors.claim: A month-8 proxy should not be assumed to predict the 48-month score without measuring the link.
errors.problem: Correct, but the research gives no way to measure the link, no threshold and no decision rule. It also misses two structural points. First, Prentice's operational criterion (the outcome is independent of treatment given the surrogate) fails by construction when policies differ in what they do after month k, because a month-k state cannot carry the effect of decisions not yet taken. Only meta-analytic, between-policy predictive validity is possible, and only per family. Phase-switching specialists (problem C) are exactly where it breaks. Second, surrogates can mislead in both directions (the surrogate paradox; CAST). Also, month 8 falls mid-window: reviews and promotions happen at 6-month boundaries, and level only changes there.
errors.correction: Adopt meta-analytic validation: between-policy association (Kendall tau or R^2_trial) with CIs, and a surrogate-threshold-effect-style prediction interval. Add a decision-level shadow-screening test. Place checkpoints right after the review windows, make validity family-specific, and exempt policies whose rules activate late. Details in the protocol.
evidence: Burzykowski & Buyse 2006 Pharm Stat 5(3):173-186 doi:10.1002/pst.207 (surrogate threshold effect)
Chen, Geng, Jia 2007 JRSS-B 69(5):919-932; VanderWeele 2013 Biometrics 69(3):561-565 (surrogate paradox)
rules.rst.txt: promotion window every six months

errors.claim: Implicitly treats an 'early score' as something available to screen on.
errors.problem: The game produces no score during a run. Any 'early score' is a proxy the team builds. Building one by fitting visible state to quantitative_score across runs is a cross-run fitted predictive model, and that is exactly pending organiser question B4. The fit could use exit states of early-terminated episodes, or Matteo's locally observed ending weights of 30/20/15/15/10/10. The research does not link partial screening to B4, nor to the ban on presenting unpublished formulas as rules.
errors.correction: Until B4 is answered, use only raw, pre-registered summaries of visible state as proxies: alive at k, level, review grades, wealth. Keep them lab-only. Do no fitted score reconstruction, and never put proxy weights into Skills.
evidence: competition-rules.rst.txt: prohibits unpublished formulas/score calculations presented as known rules, regardless of how obtained
origin/Matteo:docs/exploratory-findings.md §5 (pilot ending weights; flagged there as non-rules)

errors.claim: The concern is policies that start badly and pay off later.
errors.problem: This treats only one direction. The official docs say risks may accumulate over several months before consequences become visible, and that 'Defuse legacy risk' has no published direct statistical effect. So visible-stat proxies also produce false promotions through late costs: hidden-risk consequences, capability dismissal or 'Obsolete', and rising tokens per month as context grows. Only strategy-dossier.md §10 notes that defusing legacy risk is undervalued by a visible-delta metric, and the lab design does not carry that point into evaluation.
errors.correction: Treat every proxy as two-sided. Log cause-specific cumulative incidence after month k, and tokens/month by month. A screen may only deprioritize; it can never promote or confirm.
evidence: quickstart.rst.txt: 'Risks may accumulate over several months before their consequences become visible'
rules.rst.txt Energy actions: Defuse legacy risk, cost 2, 'No published direct statistical effect'
failure-and-ending.rst.txt: accumulated hidden risks; skill falling behind expectations

errors.claim: Iteration limits must not fabricate results or hide truncated episodes.
errors.problem: The research does not separate truncation on the actor or runtime side from infrastructure interruption. Actor-side truncation covers max-turns, context overflow, compaction, the agent ending its turn, and any JiuwenSwarm iteration cap. In the target runtime, an agent that stops at month 20 is probably scored from the state at exit ('an early exit still receives one'). That is a real, policy-attributable late failure: verbose policies hit context limits late. In a Claude Code worker, the same event is an artifact of the actor. Logging either as 'censored' hides a late-phase failure mode that differs by actor (problem A x B).
errors.correction: Make the termination category an enum: completed_48 / game_elimination:<official label> / runtime_agent_stop / operational_interruption. Score runtime_agent_stop in the target runtime if the official runner scores it; treat it as resumable censoring for dev workers. In the first target run, check that the agent reaches month 48, and check what score_report.json shows if it stops early. Ask the organisers (extend C9).
evidence: failure-and-ending.rst.txt: early exit still receives a quantitative_score from the state at exit
research/budget-and-search.md §6: about 418 MCP calls per full run, which large enough to hit agent-side caps

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/protocol.md §5; design.md §12 (cheap-worker calibration on whole-episode means)
errors.claim: The calibration matrix measures ranking agreement across actors.
errors.problem: Fidelity by phase is not addressed. Context growth and compaction degrade instruction-following as the months pass, so the divergence between cheap worker and target probably concentrates late (for example, missing a mode switch after promotion, or forgetting an early commitment). Whole-episode correlation hides this, and a late benefit may appear only with a capable actor.
errors.correction: Log compliance per month (invalid or unaffordable actions, ignored warnings, mode-switch adherence, context size) and compare actor x phase (months 1-12, 13-24, 25-48) as well as whole episodes.
evidence: design.md §12 states fidelity may vary for long or specialised candidates but proposes no phase-level check

confirmed.claim: The default evaluation unit is the complete episode; do not cut at month 8 or 12 to save cost (from-zero-lab.md §4 line 55; strategy-dossier.md §13; README conclusion 2; design.md §8).
confirmed.evidence: Hyperband's own §4.4.3 failure case; short-horizon bias (Wu et al. 2018); LC-PFN's reported failure on curves with an inflection point; the official quickstart warns that consequences can appear months later.

confirmed.claim: Early exits are scored and must not be dropped; interrupted episodes are not imputed; in-flight jobs are not observations (mathematics.md §9-10; lab-spec in_flight_jobs_are_not_observations).
confirmed.evidence: failure-and-ending.rst and competition-rules.rst: an early exit still receives quantitative_score from the state at exit.

confirmed.claim: Comparing E[Q | T>=8] is not a comparison of global performance; E[Q] = P(T>=8)E[Q|T>=8] + P(T<8)E[Q|T<8] (mathematics.md §12). The survivor_selection counterexample is correct arithmetic.
confirmed.evidence: 0.2*90+0.8*10 = 26 and 0.9*70+0.1*20 = 65; the law of total expectation.

confirmed.claim: Cause frequencies in the random batch reflect competing risks and survival length, not importance (matteo-branch-review.md; from-zero-lab.md §5B).
confirmed.evidence: Competing-risks theory: 1-KM per cause overestimates cumulative incidence, and early causes hide later ones (Putter, Fiocco, Geskus 2007 Stat Med 26:2389-2430).

confirmed.claim: A one-step visible-delta metric undervalues 'Defuse legacy risk' (strategy-dossier.md §10).
confirmed.evidence: rules.rst.txt: cost 2, no published direct statistical effect; failure-and-ending.rst lists accumulated hidden risks and a 'Risk control' ending dimension.

confirmed.evidence: mcp.rst.txt documents only new_game/observe/take_action/check_latest_logs/show_employee_handbook, with no clone, seed or undo.

confirmed.claim: The token-efficiency arithmetic is correct: 24M tokens is the full-mark boundary and 144M the zero boundary over 48 months; 1M tokens/month gives TE 80 (budget-and-search.md §3).
The zero-failure upper bounds 1-0.05^(1/n) are 63.2%, 25.9% and 9.5% for n = 3, 10, 30 (strategy-dossier.md §14).
confirmed.evidence: Direct computation.

recommendations.recommendation: Make U = 0.8*Q + 0.1*TE (published formula, 50 cap when months < 48) the primary per-run outcome for target-runtime episodes. Report Q, months survived, P(T=48), RMST(48) and tokens/month as pre-registered auxiliaries. Update lab-spec.json, experiment-registry.json and the evaluation record.
recommendations.rationale: Survival to 48 is itself worth up to 5 automated points through the TE cap, and a late-benefit policy that completes earns both. A Q-only metric ranks policies differently from the official objective.

recommendations.recommendation: No truncation of running LLM-actor episodes during 26 Oct-1 Nov. Partial (in-progress) information may only set the priority of the next launch. It is never used for dormancy, rejection, promotion or confirmation. Set worker-side caps (max-turns, timeouts) so they cannot bind before month 48.
recommendations.rationale: A truncation screen saves only E[(min(T,48)-k)+] months per episode, which falls almost entirely on long survivors, the policies whose late benefits matter. Policies that fail early truncate themselves for free. Validating a screen (see the gate) needs more complete target episodes than USD 50 is likely to buy. Scripted actors finish a full episode in seconds (about 5 random sessions/s in Matteo's harness), so they gain nothing from truncation.
evidence: Hampson & Jennison 2013 (gains from interim looks shrink with delay unless a correlated short-term endpoint is validated)

recommendations.recommendation: Extend records.schema.json with a per-month trajectory record and terminal fields: ending_contributions, termination_category enum, censor_month, resumed, tokens_cumulative_by_month. Make this logging mandatory for every episode on every actor.
recommendations.rationale: Every late-benefit diagnostic (crossing curves, reversal rates, surrogate validation, late-cost detection) needs trajectories. Collecting them costs nothing at run time, because the data comes from observe() and the run's own events-*.jsonl and score_report.json outputs, which the rules allow participants to inspect.
evidence: competition-rules.rst.txt: participants may inspect outputs generated by their own runs

recommendations.recommendation: Handle operational interruptions explicitly. Resume the same session where possible and flag it. Otherwise censor at the last month and analyse with KM, Aalen-Johansen and IPCW, plus best/worst bounds. Monitor whether censoring depends on month, and stop making decisions while censoring is informative.
recommendations.rationale: Complete-case analysis under length-dependent interruption is biased against long-surviving policies.

recommendations.recommendation: Binding closed-round rule: dormancy or rejection is decided only after all episodes launched for that policy in the round are resolved. Pending episodes appear only as right-censored rows in interim KM displays.
recommendations.rationale: Early arrivals are early exits, so asynchronous interim means are pessimistic for late-benefit policies.

recommendations.recommendation: Run randomized, stratified audits of dormant candidates every round. Use a seeded draw of max(1, 20%) of the policies made dormant in that round, stratified by reason. Each audited policy gets 2 fresh complete episodes on the actor that made the decision. If the decision rested on a cheap actor, add at least 1 target episode, prioritising 'late-shape' policies. Report the false-rejection rate with a Clopper-Pearson bound.
recommendations.rationale: This is the only direct measure of false rejection. Problem B predicts that false rejections concentrate among high-variance, late-paying policies.
evidence: design.md §12 and mathematics.md §7 already require audits of cheap-worker rejections, without design or stopping rules

recommendations.recommendation: Use a termination taxonomy that separates runtime_agent_stop from operational_interruption. In the first target-runtime episode, check that the agent actually reaches month 48, and record how score_report.json treats an agent that stops early.
recommendations.rationale: If JiuwenSwarm or deepseek-v4-flash stops before month 48 because of iteration or context limits, that late failure dominates every other late-benefit question, and it differs by actor.
evidence: research/budget-and-search.md §6 (~418 MCP calls per full run)
failure-and-ending.rst.txt (early exit scored from state at exit)

recommendations.recommendation: Pre-register and always run a shadow surrogate analysis, even if screening is never enabled. Checkpoints k are the first observation after each half-year review (months 6, 12, ..., 42). Use simple surrogates (alive, level, A/S review count, wealth, a rank composite). Metrics: Kendall tau with a two-level bootstrap, pairwise reversal rate among |dU| >= delta pairs, top-1 retention, and shadow regret.
recommendations.rationale: This turns 'do not assume month-k predicts month-48' into evidence. Either result makes a concrete, honest story for the expert-review video and design report (topic 2: what logs taught).
evidence: Stallard 2010 Stat Med 29(9):959-971 (selection on a short-term endpoint, confirmation on the long-term endpoint)

recommendations.recommendation: Add survival-analysis outputs for each policy x actor x epoch: KM with Greenwood CIs, Aalen-Johansen cause-specific CIFs, and RMST at tau = 12, 24, 48 with differences. Add death-absorbed mean trajectories for Level and Wealth, and use RMST differences rather than hazard ratios.
recommendations.rationale: Late benefits show up as crossing survival curves or trajectories. Hazard ratios assume proportional hazards and are misleading when curves cross. RMST(48) equals expected survival_months, the TE denominator.
evidence: Royston & Parmar 2013 BMC Med Res Methodol 13:152

recommendations.recommendation: Monitor late costs: tokens/month by month (test whether it grows with survival under context accumulation), cumulative incidence of late causes after month k, and actor x phase compliance.
recommendations.rationale: Under a no-compaction growth model, tokens/month rises roughly linearly with months survived, so TE measured at month k overstates final TE. Hidden risks surface late by design.

recommendations.recommendation: Use the phase profile to drive mutation. Policies with high E[U | completion] but high early hazard are 'repair' or recombination targets: keep their late-phase logic and graft early-phase safety from a policy with low early hazard. Any such repair is evaluated only with complete episodes.
recommendations.rationale: This links problem B to the existing generate/recombine/revive actions without truncation, and gives archive reopening a principled 'late-shape' signal.
evidence: design.md §4, §8-9 (recombine and revive actions; reopening reasons)

recommendations.recommendation: Use a lag ledger to guard credit assignment in trace diagnosis. For every review, promotion, warning and termination, list the decisions and quarterly allocations of the preceding 6 months. Require the orchestrator to state at least one lagged hypothesis (lag of at least one review window) alongside the proximate one.
recommendations.rationale: Evaluating whole policies by full-episode returns is unbiased regardless of delay. The mutation operator, however, works like myopic TD credit and tends to blame the last salient event. RUDDER shows TD-style estimates become biased and Monte Carlo estimates high-variance as reward delay grows.
evidence: Arjona-Medina et al. RUDDER, NeurIPS 2019, arXiv:1806.07857
GEPA-style trace reflection is the planned mutation operator (design.md §14)

recommendations.recommendation: If any staged elimination is ever used, hedge with a no-truncation, no-cut lane holding at least 30% of the evaluation budget (Hyperband's s=0 bracket).
recommendations.rationale: This bounds the loss from an uninformative low-resource signal, as in Hyperband's bracket hedging.

recommendations.recommendation: Consider 'freeze-thaw' of sessions instead of killing them. A deprioritised episode is paused (no take_action) and resumed later through observe(session_id) and check_latest_logs if its policy is reopened. This requires the policy's within-episode memory to be recoverable from notes and logs, and must first be verified through the interface and with the organisers.
recommendations.rationale: It makes screening reversible and gives free audit data without state cloning.
evidence: mcp.rst.txt: take_action records an agent note; check_latest_logs and the logs:// resource expose the session log
Swersky et al. 2014 (freeze-thaw as a concept; its curve model does not transfer)

recommendations.recommendation: Treat the three official runs at each score release as extra complete, never-truncated target evidence. Submitting at each cutoff carries little score risk because Stage 1 takes the maximum over versions.
recommendations.rationale: These are scarce full-horizon target episodes on the official configuration, though hosting differences apply.
evidence: competition-rules.rst.txt: Stage 1 = highest valid automated version score; each version is scored on three runs

recommendations.recommendation: Add the missing primary sources to bibliography.md and references.json. Hyperband §3.2/§4.4.3/§5.2 at full-text level; freeze-thaw; LC-PFN; Wu et al. 2018; Prentice 1989; Buyse et al. 2000; Burzykowski & Buyse 2006; Fleming & DeMets 1996; Chen et al. 2007; VanderWeele 2013; Stallard 2010; Hampson & Jennison 2013; Royston & Parmar 2013; Putter et al. 2007; Bang & Tsiatis 2000; RUDDER.
recommendations.rationale: Each claim the lab makes about late benefits would then rest on a primary source.
evidence: research/hierarchical-lab/bibliography.md R29-R31 read only at abstract level

audit.concrete_protocol:
0. SCOPE. This applies to every policy x actor x epoch cell. Pre-register sections 1-6 as a decision record before the first calibration data is seen. The thresholds are lab parameters, not game rules.

1. ENDPOINTS (per run r)
- Q_r = quantitative_score (0-100).
- T_r = months survived (1-48).
- Termination category C_r: completed_48 | game_elimination:<official label> | runtime_agent_stop | operational_interruption(censor_month).
- tokens_r is the target runtime's total; TE_r = clip(100*(3e6 - tokens_r/T_r)/2.5e6, 0, 100), capped at 50 if T_r < 48, and 0 if a count is missing.
- U_r = 0.8*Q_r + 0.1*TE_r, defined for target-runtime runs only.
- Policy estimands: mu_U (primary, target), mu_Q, p48 = P(T=48), RMST(tau) = integral from 0 to tau of S(t) dt for tau in {12, 24, 48} (RMST(48) = E[min(T,48)], the TE denominator), and cause-specific CIF_c(t).
- Descriptive decomposition: mu_U = p48*E[U|T=48] + (1-p48)*E[U|T<48]. Use it to locate uncertainty only, not as a causal comparison.
- Minimum relevant improvement delta_U = 4 automated points (about 5 Q points), fixed before data. Revise only by a new pre-registered decision once the per-run SD is observed.

2. LOGGING (all actors, all episodes)
(a) At the first observe() of each month m: alive, Level, CurrentLevelDuration, Health, Dignity, Skill, Network, Output, Wealth, Energy; cumulative input, output and cached tokens; context size at the last call; any compaction event; tool calls; invalid or unaffordable action attempts.
(b) Per quarter: the ordered Energy actions and the main action.
(c) Per half-year: review grade, promotion yes/no, level before and after, and whether feedback arrived before or after that quarter's actions.
(d) Warnings: month, plus a category mapped to the public failure directions (health, dignity, hidden-risk/organisational, performance, network, wealth, skill). Never record event IDs as answer keys.
(e) Terminal: score_report.json dimension contributions, the official termination label, C_r, censor_month, resumed flag.
(f) Policy mode switches, if the policy defines modes.
Source: observe() plus the run's own transcript, events-*.jsonl and score_report.json. Never the sqlite DB.

3. RUN EXECUTION
- No truncation of running LLM episodes.
- Worker caps: initially max tool calls >= 1,000 and wall-clock timeout >= 3x the median measured full-episode time.
- A cap hit is runtime_agent_stop. In the target runtime it is scored as the official runner scores it (verify on the first run). For dev workers it is resumable censoring.
- After an ambiguous take_action, observe or check logs before retrying.
- After a crash, resume the same session_id (or use the runner's --continue for the target) and set resumed=true. Run sensitivity analyses with and without resumed episodes.

4. ANALYSIS AND DECISION RULES
(a) Round closure: dormancy or rejection of policy i only when every episode launched for i in the round is resolved. Interim data may only reorder the launch queue. Pending episodes are right-censored at their current month in KM displays and never enter means.
(b) Censoring: KM with Greenwood CIs; Aalen-Johansen CIFs (not 1-KM per cause); IPCW mean of U with weights 1/G_hat(T_r), where G_hat is the KM of censoring by month; best/worst bounds that impute censored U as the policy's min and max observed U among episodes surviving past censor_month. Freeze decisions for a policy if more than 10% of its episodes are censored, or if the censoring rate in months 25-48 is at least 2x the rate in months 1-24.
(c) Dormancy: requires at least 3 resolved complete episodes and an interval criterion (upper bound of mu_U,i < mu_U,lead - delta_U, at the error level set in the statistics dimension). A 'late-shape' flag (RMST(48) in the top third of the round, or any completed episode with U >= the leader's mean) raises the minimum to 5 episodes.
(d) Survival displays per cell: KM; CIF by cause; RMST(12, 24, 48) with bootstrap CIs over episodes; death-absorbed mean Level(t) and Wealth(t), where dead episodes keep their exit value; tokens/month against months survived.

5. SHADOW SURROGATE ANALYSIS (always on; never acts by itself)
- Checkpoints k = first observation after the reviews at months 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42.
- Candidate surrogates per policy: S_k^alive = S(k); S_k^level = death-absorbed mean level at k; S_k^rev = mean count of A/S grades through k; S_k^wealth = death-absorbed mean wealth at k; S_k^comp = mean of the within-round ranks of the previous four. No fitted score model unless organiser question B4 is answered.
- Metrics across policies with complete data:
  (i) Kendall tau_b between policy means of S_k and mu_U, with a two-level bootstrap (resample policies, then episodes) and a 90% CI;
  (ii) reversal rate = share of policy pairs with |dmu_U| >= delta_U where sign(dS_k) != sign(dmu_U);
  (iii) top-1 retention = whether 'keep the top half by S_k' would have kept each round's eventual best;
  (iv) shadow regret = mu_U(best) - mu_U(best kept);
  (v) savings fraction f_k = sum of (min(T,48)-k)+ divided by sum of min(T,48).
- Report by actor and family class.

6. SCREENING GATE (truncation or no-launch on proxy). Every condition must hold within the same actor x epoch:
(G1) at least 12 policies with at least 3 complete episodes each (at least 36 complete episodes), covering the family types to be screened;
(G2) the lower 90% bound of tau_b is >= 0.5. With 12 policies the null SE of tau is about 0.22, so observed tau must be about 0.85 or more. With 8 policies the SE is about 0.29 and the gate cannot pass;
(G3) in every closed round so far, top-1 retention held and the maximum shadow regret was <= delta_U/2;
(G4) a policy is screened only if the 95% prediction interval for its final dU versus the leader, from the across-policy regression on S_k (STE logic), lies entirely below -delta_U;
(G5) exemption: policies whose text activates behaviour after k (post-promotion modes, late protection, deferred investment) are never screened at k unless that type is in the validation set;
(G6) f_k >= 0.3, otherwise screening is not worth it;
(G7) at least 30% of the evaluation budget stays in a no-truncation lane;
(G8) a seeded random 25% (minimum 1) of screened-out episodes continue to termination as an audit;
(G9) auto-disable on any audited screened-out policy within delta_U of the leader, or a rolling reversal rate above 20%.
Evaluate the gate at most twice in the week, to limit repeated looks. Expected status: closed on the target actor this week. If a full target episode costs a few USD, the key buys roughly 10-20 complete target episodes, which is below G1. For scripted actors the gate is irrelevant because full episodes take seconds. For Claude workers it may open late in the week but does not transfer to the target without its own validation.

7. AUDIT OF DISCARDED CANDIDATES
- At each round close, a seeded draw of max(1, 20%) of the policies made dormant in that round, stratified by reason: low mean / cheap-actor-based / interim / screened.
- Each gets 2 fresh complete episodes on the deciding actor. Cheap-actor-based dormancy also gets at least 1 target episode, with late-shape policies first.
- A false rejection is recorded when the updated interval reaches mu_U,lead - delta_U (or, in a Bayesian setup, P(mu_i >= mu_lead - delta_U) >= 0.2).
- Report the false-rejection rate with a Clopper-Pearson bound. After at least 5 audits, if the upper 90% bound exceeds 0.25, raise the dormancy minimum by 2 episodes and disable any screen.
- Late-shape dormant policies go first in the reopening queue.

8. DIAGNOSIS AND CREDIT ASSIGNMENT
- Each trace summary given to the orchestrator includes a lag ledger: for each review, promotion, warning and termination, the decisions and quarterly packages of the preceding 6 months.
- Every proposed mutation states a proximate and a lagged hypothesis and names the trajectory signal that would refute it.
- Mutations are evaluated only with complete episodes.
- Repair/recombination targets: high E[U|T=48] with high early hazard (months 1-12).

9. METHOD ABLATION
- At equal budget, compare: full-episode-only vs gate-enabled screening; closed-round vs naive asynchronous decisions; audit on vs off.
- Outcome: the best mu_U confirmed on fresh complete target episodes after freezing.
failure_evidence: Any audited dormant or screened-out policy, re-run to termination on fresh episodes, comes within delta_U of the leader or beats it (a confirmed false rejection).
Kendall tau_b between the policy-mean month-k surrogate and mu_U has a 90% lower bound below 0.5, or more than 20% of policy pairs with |dmu_U| >= delta_U reverse sign between S_k and the final U.
A screen at k would have dropped a round's eventual best policy (top-1 retention fails), or shadow regret exceeds delta_U/2.
Kaplan-Meier curves of two policies cross after k (the sign of S_i(t) - S_j(t) changes with an absolute difference of at least 0.15 on both sides), or RMST over [0,k] and over [0,48] differ in sign.
Death-absorbed mean Level(t) or Wealth(t) trajectories cross after a review window: the policy behind at month 12 leads at month 48.
Cause-specific cumulative incidence of late causes (hidden-risk organisational consequence, capability dismissal, Obsolete) rises after month k among policies ranked high at k (late costs).
Interim policy means taken at 50% of episodes resolved are systematically lower than closed-round means, and the gap grows with RMST(48) (asynchrony/pending bias).
The censoring rate rises with month (months 25-48 at least 2x months 1-24), or censored episodes have longer exposure than terminal ones (informative censoring makes complete-case means biased).
Tokens/month at month k underestimates the final tokens/month (TE measured early overstates final TE), for example tokens/month increasing roughly linearly with months survived.

Compliance errors for the cheap worker (invalid or unaffordable actions, ignored warnings, missed mode switches) rise after month 24 while the target's do not, or vice versa; or the surrogate-to-final relationship differs significantly by actor.
Target-runtime episodes stop before month 48 for runtime reasons (runtime_agent_stop), which shows that late-phase evaluation on non-target workers does not represent the target.

In the policy-level decomposition, a policy with lower p48 has higher E[U | T=48] and a higher overall mu_U than the one ranked higher on survival-to-k, which means survival is not a valid surrogate either.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. lab-spec.json:74 sets primary_outcome to the 'mean terminal quantitative_score under target actor'. mathematics.md §1 sets Y = quantitative_score/100. experiment-registry.json E01-E03 use primary_metric 'mean_terminal_quantitative_score', and E01's secondary metrics include 'cost' but not TE or tokens/month. competition-rules.rst.txt computes TE per run from total_tokens/survival_months and states 'A run that ends before month 48 is capped at 50 on this term'. The arithmetic checks out: completion adds up to 50 TE points, which is 5 automated points or 6.25 Q-equivalents, and 1M tokens/month gives TE = 80. research/strategy-dossier.md §2 writes A = 0.8*meanQ + 0.1*D + 0.1*E but still says early exits 'still receive a quantitative outcome' and never notes the completion bonus that the TE cap creates. Two mitigations: experiment-plan.md §2 does list 'Total tokens and survival months — compute published token efficiency' as a tracked metric, and mathematics.md §1 says optimising mu is 'one component'. The gap is therefore in the primary estimand, not in data collection. The implementation draft repeats it: /Users/alejandrotreny/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/Github/huawei/careerlab/episode.py EpisodeResult has quantitative_score but no TE.
verdicts.refined_correction: For target-runtime episodes, the primary per-run outcome is U = 0.8*Q + 0.1*TE. TE = clip(100*(3e6 - tokens/T)/2.5e6, 0, 100), capped at 50 when T < 48. Correction to the auditor: when the token count is missing because of our own instrumentation, mark U as missing and do not score TE as 0. The published zero rule applies to official runs, which will always have a runner-side count. Until organiser question C7 says which token fields count (cached, reasoning, retries), compute TE under both inclusive and exclusive accounting and report both. Report Q, T, P(T=48) and tokens/month as auxiliaries. For non-target actors, report Q and survival only.

verdicts.reason: The structural gap is real. records.schema.json $defs.evaluation (lines 172-400) has additionalProperties:false and no fields for per-month trajectory, review grades, warnings, quarterly allocations, ending-dimension contributions or tokens by month. termination_reason is free text. This is inconsistent with experiment-plan.md lines 23 and 28 and with from-zero-lab.md line 159 ('Por transición'). The auditor overstates the consequence, though. The schema is not the whole persistence contract. protocol.md §6 ('conservar trayectoria y resumen'), §7 (worker output includes evidence references and a summary of warnings and mode changes) and §8 (local-runs/<evaluation-id>/ raw evidence) keep raw trajectories, and the evaluation record links to them through evidence_ref. The untracked implementation /Users/alejandrotreny/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/Github/huawei/careerlab/episode.py already writes every observe() payload to trajectory.jsonl. So it is false that 'no month-k surrogate can be validated after the fact', provided raw evidence is retained. What is missing is a structured, validated derived record. For censored records the schema leaves survival_months unconstrained, so it could hold a censor month, but those semantics are undefined.
verdicts.refined_correction: Keep raw evidence as the single source of truth and make retaining it mandatory for every episode. Add a derived, deterministically regenerable 'trajectory' record: one row per month boundary, review and quarterly phase, with visible stats, level, CurrentLevelDuration, review grade, promotion, warnings, quarterly package and cumulative tokens when the runtime exposes them. Add terminal fields: ending_contributions (from score_report.json or the terminal observe payload), termination_category as an enum, censor_month and resumed. Define what survival_months means for each status.

verdicts.reason: The estimator gap is confirmed. lab-spec.json:73, mathematics.md §9 and records.schema.json label interruptions as 'censored' but specify no estimator. experiment-plan.md §5 only says to retain infrastructure failures separately, so the effective default is a complete-case mean. The length-bias argument holds: long episodes have more exposure to interruption, and fresh replacements do not remove the selection. Bang & Tsiatis 2000 (Biometrika 87:329-343) is correctly cited for IPCW of an end-of-follow-up quantity. Parts of the critique are already covered or unverified. Resumption is already in the prior design: protocol.md §9 says to observe the live session before retrying and to record an incomplete episode only if it cannot be recovered, lab-spec.json:90 sets resume_requires_live_handle_check, and the job record has live_handle_ref. Only the 'resumed' flag is new. The 'runner's --continue' option does not appear in the fetched quickstart, mcp or submission docs, so it is unverified. The '-c' competition mode allows only one new_game. The proposed 'best/worst bounds' are empirical min/max values of U among survivors, which are not valid bounds.
verdicts.refined_correction: Prefer resuming the same session_id through observe() after a live-handle check, as protocol.md §9 already says, and record resumed=true. Run sensitivity analyses with and without resumed episodes, because an LLM actor that loses its in-episode context is a different execution condition. Analyse censoring by month: KM for survival, Aalen-Johansen for causes, and an IPCW mean of U as a sensitivity estimate, noting that it is unstable at n of about 3-10 per policy. Replace the 'bounds' with Manski-style bounds over the logical range of U given survival to censor_month, or call them sensitivity imputations. State the freeze rule as a count: any censored episode in a cell of fewer than 10 episodes blocks dormancy or confirmation decisions for that cell until it is resolved.

verdicts.reason: Largely confirmed. mathematics.md §10 diagnoses the bias correctly, but its remedy is a non-binding 'debería' with a weaker alternative ('decisiones que registren claramente qué resultados faltan'). That alternative does not remove the bias: recording that results are missing does not stop a decision from being driven by early-arriving early exits. protocol.md:85 allows an asynchronous planner and only suggests that batch comparison be 'facilitated'. Hampson & Jennison 2013 (JRSS-B 75(1):3-54) is correctly cited: interim efficiency gains shrink as response delay grows. The prior text already does part of what the auditor asks. mathematics.md:132 restricts pending jobs to adjusting launch priority and says they never enter means or uncertainty. The real gap is decisions made on early-terminating results, so 'major' is somewhat generous.
verdicts.refined_correction: Make it binding through a per-policy launch-order prefix rule. A dormancy or rejection decision for policy i uses only the first n episodes launched for i, and only once all n are terminal or explicitly censored. This is equivalent to the auditor's round closure but avoids global barriers and idle workers when some episodes run long. Interim data may only reorder the launch queue. Pending episodes appear only as right-censored rows in KM displays, which are for display only.

verdicts.reason: The description is accurate: experiment-plan.md lines 52-53 use 2 complete games per candidate, then keep the 'strongest two', with no interval criterion and no audit. The misranking arithmetic is correct: Phi(-5/15) = 0.37 and Phi(-10/15) = 0.25. But this is not a demonstrated problem-B error. (1) The section is labelled 'Illustrative', the 8 games are marked 'exploratory only', and the text says 'not evidence that thirty games are necessary or sufficient'. §5 forbids reading small differences as rankings, and line 58 requires selection to weigh uncertainty, completion and severe failures. (2) It uses complete games, which is the problem-B-appropriate choice; strategy-dossier.md §13 explicitly says to eliminate candidate budgets rather than truncate games. The remaining issue is generic small-sample noise, not delay bias. (3) The claim that late-benefit policies 'tend to be high-variance' has no evidence behind it. (4) The correction misframes a fixed-budget selection as hypothesis testing. With about 30 target games and sigma around 15, an interval-only cut would almost never fire. Sequential halving over episode counts is a principled fixed-budget best-arm method (Karnin et al. 2013), and equal allocation of about 4.5 games per candidate still misranks a 5-point pair about 31% of the time. In an all-target plan, 'auditing' dropped candidates is just more replication.
verdicts.refined_correction: A minor improvement, not a major fix. If the staged allocation is kept, state the selection rule: for example, do not drop a candidate whose posterior probability of being within delta of the best exceeds a pre-set level, or whose difference interval with the leader includes 0. Report the estimated probability of correct selection. Consider fewer candidates per stage. Keep the no-cut hedge only if any truncation-based screening is introduced.

verdicts.reason: Refuted as stated. The research does have a decision rule. design.md:102 says 'Episodios completos; no cortar por rendimiento parcial', mathematics.md §9 says episode count, not truncation, is the resource, and strategy-dossier.md §13 makes complete games the evaluation unit. A surrogate-validation protocol is only needed if a surrogate will be used for decisions, and the auditor's own protocol concludes the screening gate stays closed on the target this week. That confirms the prior stance; it does not reveal an error. 'Month 8' is the user's own example of deceptive specialization (problem C), used that way in design.md §10, so the objection that month 8 'falls mid-window' attacks a checkpoint the research never proposed. The surrogate-literature points (Prentice 1989, Buyse et al. 2000, Burzykowski & Buyse 2006, Chen-Geng-Jia 2007, VanderWeele 2013, Fleming & DeMets 1996) are correctly cited and useful enrichment. The argument that Prentice's criterion fails when policies differ after month k is sound. That review and promotion windows are six-monthly is confirmed by rules.rst.txt. 'Level only changes there' is an unverified inference.
verdicts.refined_correction: No correction is needed to the decision stance. Optionally, add a pre-registered shadow analysis that never acts by itself, using one primary surrogate per checkpoint at the post-review months, if trajectories are retained. If screening is ever enabled, validate it meta-analytically within each family, with a surrogate-threshold-effect-style prediction interval, as the auditor describes.
