recommendation_objections: Rec 1 and protocol §1, 'TE = 0 if a count is missing': in the lab, a missing token count is our instrumentation failing, not the official zero rule. Scoring it as 0 would push U down for episodes that are merely badly logged. Treat it as missing. Also compute TE under both inclusive and exclusive token accounting until organiser question C7 is answered.

Rec 2 and protocol §3, worker caps (max tool calls >= 1,000; timeout >= 3x median): these must apply only to dev workers. For target-representative runs, participants must not alter the pinned JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 configuration, and the official runtime's caps are part of the scored environment. Raising them locally would make target evidence unrepresentative. Design the Skill to finish within the official limits instead.

Protocol §4(c) dormancy rule ('upper bound of mu_U,i < mu_U,lead - delta_U') compares a candidate's upper bound with the leader's point mean. That ignores the leader's own uncertainty and its upward selection bias (winner's curse). It is weaker than the rule already in mathematics.md §4 (the candidate's upper bound below a contender's lower bound). Use a difference interval or the leader's lower bound. At n = 3-5 and sigma around 15, expect it to almost never fire on the target, and say so.

Protocol §7 audit trigger is degenerate at this week's scale. With zero false rejections, the Clopper-Pearson one-sided 90% upper bound is 1 - 0.1^(1/n), which is 0.37 at n = 5 and only falls to 0.25 at n of about 8-9. So 'after >= 5 audits, if the upper 90% bound exceeds 0.25, raise the minimum and disable screens' fires automatically. The false-rejection definition ('updated interval reaches mu_lead - delta_U') is also met by almost any audited policy at n of about 5, because intervals are wide. That inflates the measured false-rejection rate. Define false rejection by a point estimate or posterior probability, and choose a threshold that can be reached at the planned audit count.

Protocol §4(b) censoring: the 'best/worst bounds' (the policy's empirical min/max U among survivors past censor_month) are not valid bounds. Use the logical range of U given survival to censor_month, or call them sensitivity imputations. IPCW weights from a KM of censoring are unstable with 3-10 episodes per policy and one or two censored. The '>10% censored' freeze rule amounts to 'any censored episode' at n < 10, so state it as a count. The 'runner's --continue' option does not appear in the fetched official docs, so verify it before relying on it.

Protocol §5-6 shadow surrogate analysis: 7 checkpoints x 5 surrogates x several metrics creates a multiplicity problem, and post-hoc picking of the best-looking surrogate will overstate validity. Pre-register one primary surrogate per checkpoint, or adjust. In G2, the null-variance SE of tau (0.22 for 12 policies, 0.29 for 8) is not the right SE for a confidence interval around a non-null tau; use the bootstrap the protocol already specifies. 'With 8 policies the gate cannot pass' is false: tau = 1 gives about 1 - 1.645*0.289 = 0.52 >= 0.5.

Rec 15 (official runs as extra target evidence): official scoring uses the closed evaluation dataset (competition-rules.rst.txt prohibits 'accessing the closed evaluation dataset'; packages.rst.txt describes the dev set as the 'development (dev) validation dataset'). So official runs are a different environment epoch and cannot be pooled with dev-epoch target episodes. Releases also report a version-level automated score, which probably lacks per-run Q, months and tokens. And 'little score risk' ignores that every scored version must be a complete valid final ZIP, including presentation.mp4, and that a later unscored submission before the same cutoff supersedes an earlier one.

Rec 3 (schema extension): raw trajectories are already meant to be kept (protocol.md §6-8, evidence_ref), and careerlab/episode.py writes every observation to trajectory.jsonl. The new trajectory record should be a derived table that can always be regenerated from raw evidence, not a second, divergent source of truth. Per-month cumulative tokens may not be exposed by the JiuwenSwarm runner outputs, so mark that field optional.

Rec 6 (audits with >= 1 target episode for each cheap-actor-based dormancy): with USD 50 and no measured cost per target episode, this competes directly with confirmation and final validation (budget-and-search.md §2). Set an explicit audit budget cap and an order of priority.

Rec 2's evidence ('about 5 random sessions/s, mean 5.9 months' from origin/Matteo:docs/experiments/random-baseline-summary.json) measures random runs that never exceeded 24 months, on a locked local adapter. A 48-month scripted episode is roughly 8x longer. It is still seconds, but the figure is not full-episode throughput.

audit.dimension: Problem C: deceptive specialization (calendar vs state vs feedback vs survivorship), design.md sections 10-11, mathematics.md sections 11-12 and related text
audit.verdict_summary: The package names the right risk. design.md section 10 lists level change, new feedback, resource depletion and survivorship as explanations for a month-8 pattern, and section 11 correctly makes fresh-game comparisons of complete policies the primary comparison. The research stops there, though: it gives a warning but no experimental design. It never specifies within-episode randomization with logged probabilities, and it hedges continuation studies with 'cuando el protocolo lo permita' even though they need only a common prefix policy and an RNG, not cloning. It proposes no controls that could show a specialization is either needed or contingent on context: no always-M arm, no sham injection, no yoked or random-timing control and no time-shift placebo. It has no pre-registered decision rule, and the records schema has no decision-point fields. The proposed three-policy comparison (general, calendar, contextual) may also be unidentifiable in the dev environment. Reviews follow a fixed public six-month cadence, and CurrentLevelDuration equals elapsed months until the first promotion, so 'month 8', '8 months at level' and 'two months after the first review' are aliased in most episodes. The documents do not notice this. mathematics.md section 12 is arithmetically correct but incomplete. It omits the collider mechanism and the identity that makes randomized continuations valid: with a common prefix, the value gain equals P(reach d) times the conditional effect. The bibliography contains no causal-inference sources (no Robins g-methods, Murphy SMART, MRT/excursion effects, selection-bias DAGs or negative controls), although problem C is a textbook time-varying confounding and selection problem. design.md section 10 is also too permissive on compliance: it implies a learned month is acceptable if it is not 'presented' as an engine threshold. That conflicts with the binding rules ('how it is described' does not matter, and guidance must survive parameter changes) and with the stricter strategy-dossier.md. Verdict: the direction is right, but the method is not operational. A concrete randomized-switch protocol, aliasing diagnostics, placebo controls and a compliance gate are needed before any specialization is promoted.

errors.claim: Continuation studies will use comparable prefixes and random assignment of continuations 'when the protocol allows'. Otherwise only complete policies randomized from the start are valid.
errors.problem: This treats within-episode randomization as uncertain or optional and never designs it, though it is the standard identification tool (SMART/MRT) and needs no cloning or seed. If the prefix policy is identical across arms and the switch Z is drawn at decision point d, the arms are exchangeable given the history at d. The conditional effect among episodes that reach d is then unbiased, with no survivorship bias, and the full-policy gain is P(reach d) times that effect. The docs also never plan to log assignment probabilities, so later off-policy, IPW or embedded-regime analysis is impossible. from-zero-lab.md:164 already notes that importance weights need logged propensities, but the lab does not follow through.
errors.correction: Make 'randomized mode switch at pre-registered decision points with sealed, logged probabilities' a first-class lab action. State the identity Delta V = P(T>=d) * E[Y(1)-Y(0) | T>=d] for a common prefix. Log p, Z and pre-treatment descriptors at every decision point.
evidence: Boruvka et al. 2018 JASA (known randomization probabilities in an MRT) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6241330

errors.claim: Compare three complete policies: the general one, a calendar revision and a contextual revision. Drop a temporal rule if it does not beat a state explanation in new episodes.
errors.problem: (1) There is no always-M arm, so a contextual win could just be the main effect of mode M, and the specialization would be unnecessary. (2) There is no sham-injection, yoked/random-timing or time-shift control, so contingency cannot be separated from timing, dose or a mid-episode reminder effect. (3) The decision rule has no metric, minimum effect, alpha, multiplicity rule or equivalence handling. With small n, 'does not beat' is the default outcome. (4) The arms may be aliased. Reviews are fixed every six months (public), and the manual session saw the first review at the month-6 transition. CurrentLevelDuration equals elapsed months until the first promotion. So 'month 8', '8 months at level' and '2 months after the first review' coincide in every non-promoted episode. Fresh episodes cannot separate them unless their firing times differ, and the docs never compute that discordance.
errors.correction: Arms: never-M, always-M, calendar, structural/feedback, state, plus sham and yoked-timing controls on the cheap tier. First compute pairwise trigger discordance from base-policy logs, and declare triggers aliased when discordance is below a pre-set level. Pre-register the primary metric, delta, alpha, Holm correction and the requirement that the best specialized arm beat max(never, always) by delta_spec.
evidence: handbook.rst: review every six months; CurrentLevelDuration = months at current level
research/matteo-branch-review.md:58 (first review appeared at the month-6 transition)
Church 1964 Psych Bull 62:122-131 (yoked-control design and its caveats)

errors.claim: Nor should we present the selected month or a learned value as a revealed internal threshold.
errors.problem: This implies a dev-learned month or cutpoint may ship if it is labelled as a design preference. The binding rules make content prohibition independent of 'how it was arrived at, or how it is described'. They also require guidance to remain applicable when event order, parameter values or the dataset change, and warn against assuming a dev pattern persists. packages.rst says dev behaviour, thresholds and event composition must not be assumed identical in evaluation. A month-8 rule that pays off because of dev event composition around month 8 is effectively a 'memorised event sequence', which the rules prohibit. The sentence also contradicts strategy-dossier.md:53 ('calling a recovered constant a heuristic does not establish compliance').
errors.correction: Ship no dev-tuned month numbers or statistic cutpoints in Skills. Express triggers only through public structure (48 months, quarterly phases, six-month reviews, published grade meanings such as C = corrective action advisable) or qualitative current-run trends and warnings. Add an invariance check: would the rule still make sense if review timing or event order changed? Ask organisers before shipping any calendar-keyed mode.
evidence: competition-rules.rst 'Prohibited hard-coded answers, rules, and thresholds' (does not depend on 'how it is described')

errors.claim: A month-8 change may reflect level change, new feedback, resource depletion or survivorship.
errors.problem: Four important confounds are missing. (a) Actor-side time effects: month correlates with transcript length and position, and a mid-episode instruction can help simply by re-surfacing the Skill (a reminder effect), which is not a game mechanism. (b) Dev event-sequence artifacts: the benefit may come from which dev events cluster near month 8, which would also be a compliance problem. (c) Cutpoint selection: picking m* from about 48 months inflates false positives and the effect size. (d) Prefix dependence: an excursion effect is defined relative to the schedule before it, so a month-8 effect measured under prefix P0 need not hold after recombination. A fifth case, actor capability, is also missing: a calendar trigger may win only because the cheap worker detects calendar conditions more reliably than state conditions.
errors.correction: Add these to the confound list. Each gets a matching test: a sham-injection arm, an event-concentration diagnostic, a time-shift dose-response over switch timing, re-testing after any prefix change, and trigger-recognition accuracy per actor.
evidence: Qian et al. 2022 Psych Methods (excursion effect depends on the treatment schedule) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9276848
Liu et al. Lost in the Middle https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/records.schema.json (policy.context_gate_description free string, line ~155; evaluation record lacks decision-point fields); protocol.md:108 vs 118
errors.claim: The schema covers everything needed to continue the study. protocol.md lists events/<event-id>.json, and the schema validates five record types.
errors.problem: No record can hold decision-point data: active mode, assignment Z, probability p, stratum, pre-treatment descriptors, would-have-fired flags for every candidate trigger, sham text hash, or the worker's declared mode. Problem C analyses (IPW, WCLS moderation, discordance, placebo balance) therefore cannot be run later. The gate is unstructured free text, so triggers cannot be pre-registered. protocol.md lists an events/ directory, but the schema has no event type, which is an internal inconsistency.
errors.correction: Add a 'decision_point' record (episode_id, d_index, month, quarter, stratum, p, Z, assignment_seed_ref, descriptors{}, trigger_flags{}, injected_text_sha256, declared_mode_next, availability) and a structured 'trigger' object on policies (family, Skill wording, lab operationalization, pre-registration decision id). Add an execution_class for within-episode-randomized segmented runs.

errors.claim: 55 primary sources cover the method; R40 (options) and R41 (policytree) cover context-dependent modes.
errors.problem: A grep finds no causal-inference sources: nothing on Robins g-methods or the healthy-worker survivor effect, Murphy SMART or dynamic regimes, MRT/causal excursion effects, Hernán selection bias, principal stratification or negative controls. Problem C is exactly time-varying confounding plus selection on a post-treatment variable. Robins 1986 is literally about workers whose survival in employment confounds exposure-outcome comparisons, a close analogue of this game. R41's limitation ('needs data not supplied by the current aggregate logs') would be removed by logging propensities, which the lab never plans. R40 has review_scope 'primary_abstract' (the umass PDF is a scanned image), yet the docs rely on the body definitions.
errors.correction: Add the primary causal sources and state their applicability. Note that logged randomization makes policytree-style AIPW policy learning feasible. Re-read SPS99 sections 2 and 5 (semi-Markov options, interruption) from a text copy.
evidence: grep over research/ for robins|murphy|klasnja|boruvka|hern|SMART|collider|negative control returned nothing

errors.claim: Comparing only E[Q | T>=8] ignores the probability of reaching month 8 and the states each policy produces.
errors.problem: The decomposition is correct but the diagnosis is incomplete. Survival to month 8 is a common effect of the policy and of latent episode difficulty (event draws, hidden risk), so it is a collider. Conditioning on it biases between-policy comparisons even when P(reach) is equal. The section also omits the converse: under a common prefix with randomization at d, conditioning on reaching d is harmless. Notation drifts from Y (section 1) to Q.
errors.correction: Add the collider and selection-bias explanation. Add the identity for randomized continuations. Use Y consistently. Require all randomized episodes, early exits included, in every analysis; report survival as a secondary competing-risk outcome without conditioning on post-switch survival.
evidence: Hernán 2010 'The hazards of hazard ratios' Epidemiology 21:13-15 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/pmid/20010207
Frangakis & Rubin 2002 Biometrics 58:21-29 (survivor average causal effect)

errors.claim: Option o = (I, pi, beta). A selector picks a mode from public history. A specialization needs entry, behaviour, exit and priority.
errors.problem: The mapping is correct, but three points are missing. Priority is part of the policy over options, not the option triple. SPS99 theory is for Markov states, while this game is partially observable (hidden risks), so modes are history-based or semi-Markov. As a result, a calendar trigger can be a legitimate proxy for unobserved accumulation, not automatically spurious; the deciding criteria should be robustness to parameter change and contingency tests, not 'calendar = bad'. Finally, hysteresis or minimum dwell is a free design parameter that changes switch timing and must be pre-registered, not left as a stated preference.
errors.correction: State that modes are semi-Markov or history-based. Pre-register a minimum dwell (for example one quarter) and the exit condition. Judge calendar triggers by invariance and contingency evidence plus the compliance gate.
evidence: Sutton, Precup, Singh 1999 AIJ 112:181-211 (options induce an SMDP; interruption result in the abstract) https://all.cs.umass.edu/pubs/1999/sutton_ps_AI99.pdf

errors.claim: The survivor-selection counterexample illustrates the problem (A: 0.2*90+0.8*10=26; B: 0.9*70+0.1*20=65).
errors.problem: The arithmetic is correct, but it only shows reach-probability weighting. There is no counterexample for the deceptive part: confounding by indication (good-state games switch and win, so the switch looks causal) or aliasing (calendar and structural triggers identical in dev, divergent if the review timing changes).
errors.correction: Add two synthetic cases: (1) confounding by indication with an observational switch-outcome association but zero randomized effect; (2) aliased triggers with equal dev value and different values under a shifted review cadence.

errors.claim: If the orchestrator changes the worker's instructions mid-episode, we have defined a different interactive policy.
errors.problem: True for ad hoc orchestrator steering. But a pre-registered stochastic switch, with the rule, probability and sealed assignment fixed before the episode, is a fixed stochastic policy and not adaptive steering. As worded, the sentence discourages the key design for problem C.
errors.correction: Distinguish 'pre-registered randomized switch (fixed stochastic policy)' from 'adaptive orchestrator intervention (new interactive policy)' and label them separately in execution_class.

errors.claim: The B4-B6 questions cover learning scope.
errors.problem: No question asks whether a Skill may contain a mode switch keyed to public time structure, or to qualitative current-run feedback chosen through dev experiments. None asks whether team-chosen numeric heuristics are acceptable if not presented as engine thresholds, or whether lab-side mid-episode instruction injection for external development workers is allowed.
errors.correction: Add a targeted question with a concrete example ('after a review graded C or D, prioritise corrective delivery for the next quarter' versus 'from month 8 ...').
evidence: competition-rules.rst 'Interpretation and questions' (absence of prohibition is not permission)

errors.claim: Specialization is covered: replication, mutation, reopening and specialization are distinguished, and the ablation removes context modes.
errors.problem: This overclaims coverage. No specialization protocol exists, and the ablation has no measure of spurious specializations, such as a pipeline-level placebo estimating how often the orchestrator 'discovers' calendar rules in label-permuted traces.
errors.correction: Downgrade the claim to 'risk identified; protocol pending'. Add a false-discovery audit of the specialise operator to the ablations.

confirmed.claim: The primary comparison must be between complete policies started from fresh games. Comparing actions from month 8 onward across different policies mixes procedure effects with prefix-induced state.
confirmed.evidence: design.md:128-130. Valid because between-episode randomization makes arms exchangeable at baseline (standard RCT logic). Consistent with Hernán et al. 2004 on selection when conditioning on post-treatment variables.

confirmed.claim: E[Q] = P(T>=8)E[Q|T>=8] + P(T<8)E[Q|T<8], and the survivor counterexample arithmetic (26 vs 65) is correct.
confirmed.evidence: mathematics.md:148; counterexamples.json:42-55. Recomputed: 0.2*90+0.8*10=26 and 0.9*70+0.1*20=65.

confirmed.claim: No cloning, undo or seed exists, so identical state pairs cannot be claimed.
confirmed.evidence: mcp.rst lists exactly five tools; new_game() returns a session_id with no seed parameter. mathematics.md:152 and design.md:132 are consistent with this.

confirmed.claim: Options (initiation, intra-option policy, termination) are an appropriate formal language for modes with entry and exit conditions.
confirmed.evidence: Sutton, Precup & Singh 1999 AIJ 112:181-211: options over an MDP form an SMDP, and termination conditions or interruption can improve on executing options to completion.

confirmed.claim: Named-event or quoted-situation instructions are not valid specializations.
confirmed.evidence: design.md:124 matches competition-rules.rst ('when this named event or this quoted plot situation appears, choose this option' is prohibited).

confirmed.claim: Phase awareness should be expressed as planning questions, not month-specific answers.
confirmed.evidence: strategy-dossier.md section 11 (lines 148-156) is consistent with the rule that guidance must remain applicable when event order or parameter values change.

confirmed.claim: Matteo's candidate Skills already show compliant, state-triggered modes with explicit exit conditions and no calendar keys.
confirmed.evidence: origin/Matteo:solution/skills/career-risk-review/SKILL.md ('Avoid indefinite defensive play once the reason for recovery has been addressed'). The quarterly-planning Skill uses 'remaining career horizon' qualitatively without month numbers.

confirmed.claim: Off-policy reuse of traces needs recorded actions and propensities, and Matteo's aggregates cannot support it.
confirmed.evidence: from-zero-lab.md:164; matteo-branch-review.md:10, 40 (aggregate-only; no trajectories).

recommendations.recommendation: Adopt a randomized-switch protocol for every 'specialise' action. Run the frozen base policy unchanged until a pre-registered decision point d (quarter-phase boundaries and the post-review point). Draw Z from a sealed, pre-generated sequence with p in [0.3, 0.7] (default 0.5), stratified by the lab's trigger-on/off flag. Inject either the mode-M text or a length-matched sham. Log p, Z, stratum and all pre-treatment descriptors.
recommendations.rationale: This is the only budget-feasible way to separate state dependence from timing and survivorship without cloning. A common prefix makes the effect conditional on reaching d valid, and Delta V = P(reach d) * tau_d. Logged probabilities enable IPW and embedded-regime estimation and moderation analysis.
evidence: Dempsey et al. stratified MRT https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.03587

recommendations.recommendation: Before any head-to-head test, compute from base-policy logs each trigger's firing-time distribution and the pairwise discordance D_ab. If D_ab is below a pre-set level (for example 0.1), declare the triggers aliased, record 'not separately identified in dev', and choose the public-structure or feedback wording on compliance and invariance grounds.
recommendations.rationale: Reviews follow a fixed public six-month cadence, and CurrentLevelDuration equals elapsed months until the first promotion. Calendar, level-duration and post-review triggers therefore coincide in most episodes, and only discordant episodes carry information (effective n is about n * D_ab).
evidence: matteo-branch-review.md:58 (first review at the month-6 transition)

recommendations.recommendation: Require evidence that the effect depends on context before keeping any specialization. The trigger-M regime must beat max(never-M, always-M) by a pre-registered delta_spec, and the randomized effect of M must show a qualitative interaction: positive when the trigger is on, null or negative when it is off.
recommendations.rationale: Without this, a 'specialist' may be the main effect of a generally better mode, or a quantitative-only interaction. Either way it adds complexity and execution risk for deepseek-v4-flash with no benefit over a general rule.

recommendations.recommendation: Include placebo and negative-control arms and checks on the cheap tier: a sham injection; yoked timing (switch at a time drawn from the state trigger's firing distribution, independent of the episode's own state); a time-shift dose-response (switch quarter randomized among q*-1, q*, q*+1); pre-switch balance; negative-control outcomes fixed before d; and an event-concentration diagnostic.
recommendations.rationale: These checks separate (i) LLM reminder or context effects, (ii) contingency versus timing or dose, (iii) a true calendar peak versus a step at a structural event, and (iv) dev event-sequence artifacts, which are also a compliance hazard.

recommendations.recommendation: Add a compliance gate before a specialization enters a Skill. Use only public structure or qualitative current-run feedback in the wording. Exclude dev-tuned month numbers and statistic cutpoints, event names, quoted situations and sequence positions. Present the mode as a tested team heuristic with its uncertainty. Run an invariance thought-test (would it still make sense if review timing or event order changed?). Send a specific Discord question first.
recommendations.rationale: Binding rules make prohibition independent of how content was derived or described. They require guidance to survive parameter and order changes, and they forbid memorised event sequences. design.md:124 is weaker than these rules and contradicts strategy-dossier.md:53.

recommendations.recommendation: Extend records.schema.json with a decision_point record and a structured trigger object (family, Skill wording, lab operationalization that is never shipped, pre-registration id). Add an execution_class for segmented, within-episode-randomized runs. Fix the events/ versus five-record-types inconsistency.
recommendations.rationale: Without these fields, none of the problem C analyses can be run or audited later, and triggers cannot be pre-registered.

recommendations.recommendation: Estimate with designs that exploit randomization. Use covariate-adjusted difference in means, adjusting for the pre-d state (Lin 2013), for tau_d. Use weighted-centered least squares with episode-clustered robust SEs for moderation by pre-registered descriptors. Use IPW or weighted-and-replicated estimators for embedded regimes, with weights only at mode-choice points (at most 3 randomized points per episode, so weights are at most 8).
recommendations.rationale: Pre-switch state is a pre-treatment covariate under randomization at d, and adjusting for it cuts variance by a factor of (1-R^2). Options-level importance sampling avoids the exponential variance of per-action weights over a 48-month horizon.
evidence: Murphy, van der Laan & Robins 2001 JASA 96:1410-1423 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2794446

recommendations.recommendation: Treat every specialization estimate as conditional on the prefix policy, the actor and the environment version. Re-test after any recombination or prefix change. Measure trigger-recognition accuracy per actor (worker's declared mode versus the lab's would-have-fired flag) and check that the mode was actually adopted.
recommendations.rationale: Excursion effects depend on the treatment schedule that precedes them. A calendar trigger can also 'win' only because a cheap worker detects calendar conditions more reliably than state conditions, which is a problem A and C interaction.

recommendations.recommendation: Run a pipeline-level false-discovery audit of the specialise operator. Give the orchestrator trace summaries with month or quarter labels cyclically shifted by a random offset. Count the calendar rules it proposes and how many pass the C2 and C3 gates. Include this in the protocol.md section 11 ablations alongside 'with versus without specialise at equal budget'.
recommendations.rationale: Pattern-seeking LLM orchestrators can generate plausible month rules from noise. A cutpoint chosen from about 48 months inflates the false-positive rate (Altman 1994). This audit estimates that rate directly.

recommendations.recommendation: Add the causal-inference primary sources to bibliography.md and references.json with applicability notes. Rewrite mathematics.md section 12 with the collider explanation and the randomized-continuation identity. Add confounding-by-indication and aliasing counterexamples.
recommendations.rationale: The current source base has none of the core literature for this dimension. Without it, the math explains why naive comparisons fail but not how to make valid ones.

recommendations.recommendation: For the target actor (deepseek-v4-flash in JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3), which allows no mid-episode injection, use only between-episode randomized full regimes whose texts are byte-identical apart from the trigger clause. Use them for a small pre-registered non-inferiority or rank check of R0 versus the best specialized regime, not for discovering the mechanism.
recommendations.rationale: The USD 50 key makes target-side superiority tests for context effects infeasible unless effects are large. Embedding a pre-drawn assignment token in the prompt risks the model anticipating the switch, so if used it must be checked with a pre-switch balance placebo.
evidence: api-key and competition-rules docs (designated model only, limited credit)

audit.concrete_protocol:
SPECIALIZATION PROTOCOL v0 (lab parameters, never game rules)

0. Objects. P0 = frozen base policy (sha256). Mode M = named procedure block with entry I, behaviour pi_M, exit beta and a minimum dwell of 1 quarter. Pre-register at most 4 trigger families, each with (a) Skill wording, which is shippable, qualitative and anchored in public facts, and (b) a lab operationalization used only to log would-have-fired flags, never shipped:
- T_cal: 'from month m*'. This is the hypothesis under test; it is never shipped as a number.
- T_struct: 'after the first performance review has been received'.
- T_fb: 'after a review graded C or D'. The published meaning is below expectations, corrective action advisable.
- T_state: 'when a principal visible statistic has fallen across consecutive quarterly observations, or a warning repeats'.
Descriptors logged at every decision point (all public): month, quarter, months remaining, level, CurrentLevelDuration, the 7 visible stats, last grade, review count, generic warning count in the last quarter, active mode, the worker's declared priority. Event IDs and titles are never used as descriptors or triggers.

1. Pre-registration (a decision record written before data).
- Primary outcome: Y = terminal quantitative_score of every randomized episode. Early exits count at their exit score. Operational interruptions are censored and excluded, reported, with a [0,100] bounding sensitivity analysis. Pending jobs are never counted.
- Analyse a cohort only when all of its launched episodes have terminated or been censored.
- delta_min = 3 score points (2.4 Stage-1 points). delta_spec = delta_min over max(V_never, V_always).
- Alpha = 0.05 two-sided per confirmatory family, Holm across at most 4 trigger contrasts, power 0.8.
- At most 3 looks, using O'Brien-Fleming boundaries or a betting confidence sequence (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas) on Y/100.
- Moderators: only variables measured before randomization at d. Anything else is labelled exploratory and needs fresh confirmation.

2. C1 Feasibility, base policy only. Run at least 20 terminal episodes per actor tier.
Compute: r_d = P(reach d); sigma_hat of Y; R^2 of Y on pre-d state; each trigger's firing-time distribution F_T; pairwise discordance D_ab = P(a and b fire at different d, or only one fires).
If D_ab < 0.1, declare a and b aliased and do not test them head-to-head. Pick the wording anchored in public structure or feedback (expected aliasing: month index = CurrentLevelDuration until the first promotion; month m* = m*-6 months after the first review).
Effective n for a contrast is about n * D_ab.

3. C2 Mechanism, cheap tier (Haiku/Sonnet via segmented Claude Code episodes; scripted actors only if organisers permit non-LLM drivers).
- Run one quarter per segment (claude -p --resume) with identical segment prompts in all arms.
- At each available d (at most K=3 randomized points per episode), compute the stratum S_d (trigger on/off). Draw Z_d ~ Bernoulli(p_S), p in [0.3, 0.7], default 0.5, from a sequence sealed in the job record before the episode starts.
- Inject the M text if Z=1, or a length-matched sham if Z=0 (e.g. 'Continue your current procedure; restate your current priority in one sentence').
- Controls in the same experiment: a time-shift arm randomizing the switch quarter among {q*-1, q*, q*+1}, and a yoked-timing arm switching at a time drawn from F_T(T_state) regardless of the episode's state.
- Estimands and estimators:
  - tau_d = E[Y | Z=1, reach d] - E[Y | Z=0, reach d], estimated with Lin-adjusted difference in means on the pre-d state. Delta V = r_d * tau_d.
  - Moderation tau(S) by weighted-centered least squares with episode-clustered SEs.
  - Embedded regimes (never; always-from-d1; trigger-only) by IPW or weighted-and-replicated estimators, with weights only at mode-choice points (at most 8).
- Specialization is supported only with a qualitative interaction (Gail-Simon): tau(on) > 0 and tau(off) <= 0, and V_trigger - max(V_never, V_always) >= delta_spec with confidence.
- Checks:
  - Pre-d balance must be exact; a failure means an assignment leak or anticipation.
  - Manipulation check: rubric-scored adoption of M within the next quarter.
  - Trigger-recognition accuracy: declared mode versus lab flag.
  - Negative-control outcomes fixed before d.
  - Event-concentration diagnostic: is the benefit concentrated in episodes with particular dev events near m*? If so, reject the rule as a dataset artifact.

4. Sample size, driven by observed variability and recomputed at each look.
- Regime arms: n per arm = 2(1.96+0.84)^2 * sigma_hat^2 * (1-R^2) / delta^2, about 15.7 * sigma_hat^2 * (1-R^2) / delta^2. Unadjusted examples: sigma 10, delta 3 gives 174 per arm; delta 5 gives 63; sigma 15, delta 5 gives 141.
- Within-episode, single d, 1:1: N_total = 4(1.96+0.84)^2 * sigma_d^2 * (1-R^2) / (r_d * tau_d^2).
- If the projected N for delta_spec exceeds the remaining budget, stop and mark the candidate 'dormant: not identifiable within budget'. That is not a rejection.

5. C3 Confirmation, fresh games.
- Freeze the arms, byte-identical apart from the trigger clause: R0 (never), R_always, R_best-trigger, plus R_cal only if not aliased. Randomize between episodes and size the cheap-tier run as in step 4. Use no C2 episodes.
- Then run the target actor (deepseek-v4-flash, JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3, mode agent) on R0 versus R_best as a pre-registered small non-inferiority check (margin -delta_min), with statistics kept separate per actor x environment version.
- Promote only if cheap-tier superiority is confirmed and target non-inferiority is not contradicted.
- Re-run C2 or C3 after any prefix change or recombination.

6. C4 Pipeline placebo and ablation.
- Give the orchestrator traces with month or quarter labels cyclically shifted by a random offset. Record the rate of calendar-rule proposals and their C2/C3 pass rate; this is the operator's false-discovery estimate.
- Ablation: the full lab with versus without the specialise action at equal budget. Metrics: best confirmed policy, number of specializations failing confirmation, and discovery-to-confirmation shrinkage.

7. Compliance gate, all items required to ship.
- (i) Wording uses only public structure (48 months, quarters, six-month reviews, grade meanings) or qualitative current-run trends and warnings.
- (ii) No dev-learned month numbers or statistic cutpoints.
- (iii) No event names, quoted situations or sequence positions.
- (iv) design/ documents present the mode as a tested team heuristic with evidence and uncertainty.
- (v) Invariance: the rule still makes sense if review timing, parameters or event order change.
- (vi) An organiser reply on Discord is logged whenever there is any doubt.
failure_evidence: Trigger discordance D(T_cal, T_struct) or D(T_cal, CurrentLevelDuration) near 0 in base-policy logs: a 'month m*' rule cannot be told apart from 'after the first review' or 'm* months at level', so any claim that the calendar is the mechanism is unsupported.
Randomized effect of mode M similar in trigger-on and trigger-off strata (no qualitative interaction), or V(always-M) >= V(trigger-M) within delta_spec: the specialization is unnecessary.
State-triggered regime about equal to the yoked random-timing regime: the benefit comes from timing or dose, not contingency on state.
Sham injection reproduces most of the switch's benefit: an LLM reminder or context-refresh artifact, not a game strategy.
Time-shift dose-response flat across q*-1, q*, q*+1, or showing a step at the review rather than a peak at m*: the calendar month is not the mechanism.
Effect estimated on discovery traces much larger than on fresh confirmation episodes, or the confirmation interval includes 0 or excludes delta_min (winner's curse from cutpoint search).
Effect disappears after Lin adjustment for pre-switch state, or exists only when analysis is restricted to episodes that survived past the switch (a post-treatment collider).
Effect concentrated in episodes that met particular dev events near m*: a dataset-sequence artifact, which also violates the memorised-sequence prohibition.
Effect present with Haiku but absent with Sonnet or the target, or present under prefix P0 but gone after recombination: actor-specific or schedule-dependent excursion effect.
Trigger-recognition accuracy much lower for state triggers than calendar triggers with the cheap worker: an execution-capability confound (problem A), not a strategic difference.
Pre-switch balance check fails (prefix actions or stats differ by assignment): assignment leak or anticipation, so the C2 data are invalid.
Orchestrator proposes calendar rules at a similar rate on label-shifted traces: the specialise operator generates spurious rules.
open_questions: Will organisers allow a development harness to segment Claude worker episodes and inject a randomized mode instruction mid-episode (lab only, five tools only)? This is not covered by the unsent questions A1-A2.

Will organisers accept a Skill mode switch keyed to public time structure ('after a review graded C or D', 'in the final year'), and are team-chosen numeric heuristics acceptable if not presented as engine thresholds?

What are sigma of the terminal score and P(reach month 8 or the first review) for reasoned agents per actor? Matteo's random-play aggregates (mean survival 5.91 months, no per-run distribution) cannot answer this.

Does CurrentLevelDuration start at 0 or 1 relative to the month, and does it reset exactly at promotion? This matters for the aliasing computation and must be read from observe() output, not package data.
Does JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 compact or summarize context mid-episode? That would create a calendar-correlated actor-side effect that could masquerade as a month rule.
What does a target-actor episode cost under the USD 50 key? This sets whether any target-side non-inferiority check is affordable.

Can the evaluation configuration change the review cadence or horizon? The handbook lists the time structure as public, but evaluation parameters are unpublished, which affects how robust public-structure-anchored triggers are.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. design.md:130 makes randomized continuations conditional ('cuando el protocolo lo permita'). design.md:48 classes any mid-episode instruction change as a separate 'interactive policy' and stops there. No lab action, decision enum or record field exists for assignment Z, probability p or seed (records.schema.json; the decision.action enum has 'specialise' but nothing randomized). from-zero-lab.md:164 already says importance weights need logged propensities. The auditor missed stronger evidence: experiment-plan.md section 6 says 'A genuine controlled counterfactual needs an officially supported mechanism; this MCP does not document one'. That confuses per-episode counterfactual pairing, which does need cloning, with randomized average effects, which do not. Two things push back on the auditor. First, mathematics.md:152 is a correct statement of the exchangeability condition (common prefix, assignment that does not alter the pre-switch path), so the gap is omission, not a wrong claim. Second, the identity Delta V = P(T>=d)*tau_d holds only for the lab's injected regime, which is exactly the separate 'interactive policy' of design.md:48. It is not the gain of the shippable Skill. In the Skill the trigger clause is present from month 1, so it can change pre-d behaviour (anticipation, context cost), and the target actor must recognise the trigger itself. tau_d is therefore evidence about mechanism, not about deployable value. The injection mechanism is also unverified: claude -p segments re-spawn a stdio MCP server, and whether a session survives that restart is unknown.
verdicts.refined_correction: Add 'randomized mode switch at pre-registered decision points' as a lab action for mechanism studies. Draw Z from a sealed sequence the worker cannot see before d. Log p, Z, seed reference, stratum and the injected text hash. State Delta V_lab = P(T>=d)*E[Y(1)-Y(0)|T>=d, prefix P0, actor m] and label it the effect of the injected interactive regime. Say explicitly that the shippable regime's value must come from between-episode comparisons of full Skills. Before relying on it, pilot the injection mechanism with one live session: a continuous session with a hook that injects context, or a persistent server on the CLI's http transport (ask on Discord, since mcp.rst documents stdio for other clients). Do not assume that claude -p --resume keeps the game session. Fix experiment-plan.md section 6: average causal effects need randomization, not cloning.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. design.md:120 names three arms (general, calendar, contextual) with no always-M arm, so a contextual win cannot be told apart from a main effect of M. The retention rule (line 120) has no metric, delta, alpha or multiplicity rule. It only covers temporal versus state, and never says a state rule must beat the general policy. The aliasing point holds. rules.rst and handbook.rst fix reviews and promotion windows at a six-month cadence, CurrentLevelDuration is months at the current level, and matteo-branch-review.md:58 records the first review at the month-6 transition. So 'month 8' and '2 months after the first review' coincide in every episode. Month and CurrentLevelDuration separate only in episodes promoted at the month-6 window, the only window before month 8. Three refinements. (a) The sham-injection control fits only injection designs. design.md:120 compares complete policies, so the matching control there is a length- and complexity-matched placebo clause. (b) The auditor's discordance measure ('fire at different d') mishandles triggers that are fixed shifts of each other. 'After the first review' fires at month 6 and 'from month 8' at month 8, so D=1, yet both are calendar functions under the published cadence and can never be separated as mechanisms with dev data. (c) Defaulting to the state rule when the temporal rule does not win is defensible on compliance and invariance grounds (competition-rules.rst requires guidance to survive changes in event order and parameters). The real defect is the missing never-M and always-M comparators and missing criteria, not the asymmetry itself.
verdicts.refined_correction: Arms: never-M, always-M, plus only shippable trigger families (feedback-graded and state/warning; a public-structure wording only if it differs from the calendar arm in firing time). On the cheap tier add a matched placebo clause for complete-policy runs, or a sham only in injection runs. Define aliasing for each operationalization pair as 'induces the same switch time in the episode'. Declare up front that triggers keyed to the fixed review cadence are calendar triggers and are not identified separately in dev. Pre-register the metric, delta, alpha and Holm, and require the specialised arm to beat both never-M and always-M (an intersection-union test).

verdicts.reason: Partly confirmed. design.md:120 calls the calendar arm 'una revisión que usa el calendario como preferencia de diseño'. design.md:124 then forbids only presenting the month as a 'revealed internal threshold'. Read together, they imply the framing is what matters. That is weaker than competition-rules.rst ('does not depend on ... how it was arrived at, or how it is described'), packages.rst (dev thresholds and event composition must not be assumed identical in evaluation), strategy-dossier.md:53, experiment-plan.md:86 ('learned thresholds ... remain organiser questions') and organiser-questions.md B4. The auditor overreaches in places. The binding prohibitions are named-event answers, lookup tables, memorised event sequences, and unpublished simulation thresholds or formulas presented as known rules. A team-chosen timing for the agent's own mode switch is a grey zone, not 'effectively a memorised event sequence'. Banning every 'statistic cutpoint' goes beyond the rules: they explicitly allow guidance like 'consider low health', and the SKILL.md rubric rewards 'decision criteria, including what to do near a limit'.
verdicts.refined_correction: Ship no month index or statistic cutpoint whose value was searched or tuned on dev outcomes; such a value may encode dev composition or hidden thresholds. Thresholds the team fixes before seeing data, on published scales (for example Health 0-10), stated as team safety margins and not as simulation thresholds, are permitted general strategy. Calendar wording is allowed only when anchored in public structure (48 months, quarters, six-month reviews, the final review window). Add the invariance check, and send a Discord question before shipping any calendar-keyed mode that is not derived from public structure. Edit design.md:120 and :124 to match strategy-dossier.md:53.

verdicts.reason: The confound list at design.md:118 does omit actor-side effects of time (month tracks transcript length; instructions drift), cutpoint selection, dev event-composition artifacts, prefix dependence and trigger-recognition ability. Several are partly covered elsewhere, though, so 'missing' overstates it. Cutpoint and selection inflation is countered by the fresh-episode requirement (design.md:120) and the selection discussion in mathematics.md section 3. Dev distribution shift appears at mathematics.md:160 and design.md:124. Prefix dependence appears at mathematics.md:152 and design.md:128. Actor bias appears in design.md section 12. Qian et al. 2022 does support schedule dependence: it says the excursion effect 'implicitly depends on the schedule'. 'Lost in the Middle' is a weak fit: it studies where relevant information sits in long retrieval inputs, not instruction drift over multi-turn agent episodes. The reminder effect is a confound only for interpreting mechanism, or in injection designs. In complete-policy runs it is part of the deployable effect.
verdicts.refined_correction: Add to section 10 the following confounds: (a) actor attention or instruction drift over the episode, citing Li et al. 2024 COLM https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10962 and Laban et al. 2025 https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120 instead of only Lost in the Middle; (b) dev event-composition artifacts; (c) cutpoint selection during discovery, with a pointer to the fresh-confirmation rule; (d) prefix dependence after recombination; (e) trigger-recognition accuracy per actor. Each gets a proportionate diagnostic: matched placebo or sham, an event-concentration check, varied switch timing, re-tests after prefix changes, and a declared-versus-computed trigger agreement rate.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed at the schema level. The evaluation and policy records use additionalProperties:false and no field can hold decision-point data. context_gate_description is free text. protocol.md:108 lists events/<event-id>.json, while protocol.md:118 says the schema covers five types and has no event type (protocol.json is not covered either). completion-audit.md:14 nonetheless claims persistence coverage. Two parts are overstated. 'Cannot be run later' is not true of everything: descriptors and would-have-fired flags are functions of public observations, and can be recomputed after the fact from retained trajectories (evidence_ref; per-transition logging in from-zero-lab.md:159). Recomputing them under a pre-registered operationalization is arguably better than trusting runtime flags. Only Z, p, the seed reference, the injected text hash and the worker's declared mode must be captured at run time, and they exist only once the randomized design is adopted. The events/ issue is an unschematized directory that the integrator appends to (protocol.md:122), not a logical contradiction.
verdicts.refined_correction: Add a decision_point record (evaluation_id, d_index, month, quarter, stratum, p, Z, assignment_seed_ref, injected_text_sha256, declared_mode_next, availability; descriptors and trigger flags optional, with a pointer to the trajectory span). Add a structured trigger object on policies (family, shippable wording, lab operationalization version, pre-registration decision id). Add an execution_class for segmented or injected runs. Either define an event schema or state that events/ is unvalidated. Narrow the claim in completion-audit.md:14.

verdicts.reason: The main claim holds. A grep of research/ finds no SMART, MRT, Robins, Hernán, principal-stratification or negative-control sources, although problem C is selection on a post-treatment variable plus time-varying confounding. The cited works check out: Klasnja 2015 (PMC4732571), Boruvka 2018 (PMC6241330, which says the effect depends on the treatment distribution 'in the data we have at hand'), Qian 2022 (PMC9276848) and Dempsey arXiv 1711.03587. R41's limitation would indeed go away with logged propensities. The R40 sub-claim is false, however. The UMass PDF is not a scanned image: it has an extractable text layer with embedded Times fonts, and the extracted section 2 reads 'Options consist of three components: a policy ... a termination condition ... and an initiation set'. The docs' o=(I,pi,beta) is therefore a correct reading of the body. The only problem is that the review_scope label 'primary_abstract' understates it. The 'claim' attributed to the docs is also the auditor's paraphrase: completion-audit.md:13 claims SOTA coverage in general terms.
verdicts.refined_correction: Add the primary causal sources with notes on how they apply: Murphy 2005 SMART; Klasnja 2015 and Boruvka 2018 MRT; Qian 2022; Qian 2025 distal causal excursion effects (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13500), which fits a terminal outcome better than WCLS; Robins 1986 on the healthy-worker survivor effect; Hernán et al. 2004 on selection bias; Frangakis & Rubin 2002; Lipsitch 2010. Note that logged randomization makes policytree-style doubly robust policy learning possible. For R40, update review_scope to reflect a reading of section 2 of the text-layer PDF. No re-acquisition is needed.

recommendation_objections: The randomized-switch protocol (rec. 1, C2) measures the effect of an injected interactive regime, which design.md:48 already calls a different policy. It does not measure the shippable Skill, whose clause is present from month 1 and which the target actor must detect for itself. Delta V = r_d*tau_d is therefore mechanism evidence only. The shipping decision must rest on between-episode full-Skill comparisons (C3), and the budget should be weighted that way.

The segmentation mechanism ('claude -p --resume' per quarter) is untested. Each claude -p process starts its own stdio MCP server, and whether a game session survives a server restart is unknown; it cannot be checked by reading the database. Pilot a continuous session with a context-injecting hook, or a persistent server on the CLI's streamable-http transport, before planning on it. Also check this against the still-unsent Discord questions (protocol.md:9-11, organiser-questions A1-A2). The whole external lab is still unapproved, and the protocol should list that as gate 0.

Internal inconsistency: the compliance gate forbids shipping a dev-learned month, yet C2 and C3 spend arms and Holm alpha on T_cal head-to-head contrasts. A T_cal arm cannot change what ships. Keep it at most as an exploratory diagnostic, and limit confirmatory contrasts to shippable families against max(never, always).

The discordance metric D_ab = P(fire at different d) treats triggers that are fixed shifts of each other as non-aliased. 'After the first review' (month 6) and 'from month 8' give D=1, yet under the published fixed six-month cadence both are calendar triggers and no dev data can separate them. Define aliasing per operationalization pair as 'induces the same switch time', and declare calendar and fixed-cadence structure non-identifiable as families.

'Pre-d balance must be exact' is wrong. Randomization gives balance in expectation, and finite samples will show chance imbalance. Use a pre-registered permutation or standardized-difference check, and flag only departures beyond chance.

The bound 'IPW weights at most 8' holds only when p=0.5 at all three points. With the allowed p in [0.3, 0.7] the maximum weight is (1/0.3)^3, about 37. Fix p=0.5 or report the true bound and effective sample size.

WCLS (Boruvka 2018) is built for proximal or lag-k effects. With a single terminal distal outcome and at most 3 randomizations, use a regression of Y on Z_d, Z_d x S_d and pre-d covariates with episode-clustered SEs, or the distal causal excursion effect estimator (Qian 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13500, implemented in the MRTAnalysis R package).

A sham like 'restate your current priority in one sentence' is not inert for an LLM. It is a reflection prompt and may improve play by itself. It then estimates M against reflection, not M against no change. Use a content-free length-matched sham, or add a no-injection arm.

The C4 pipeline placebo, which cyclically shifts month labels, would make reviews appear at months that contradict the published six-month cadence and CurrentLevelDuration. An orchestrator that knows the handbook may notice. Permuting outcomes across episodes, or shuffling outcome labels, while leaving traces internally consistent gives a cleaner null for the operator's false-discovery rate.

The budget is unrealistic for 26 Oct - 1 Nov on a Claude Max plan with extra usage disabled: about 174 episodes per arm at delta=3 across five or more arms, plus sham, yoked and time-shift controls, C4 placebo and an equal-budget specialise ablation, which itself needs several complete searches. Plan from the minimum detectable effect at a feasible N (for example n=30 per arm and sigma=10 give an MDE of about 7.2 points). Pre-declare that most specializations will be marked 'not identifiable within budget', and rank C2 below C3.

The target-side non-inferiority check at margin 3 points has almost no power with the USD 50 key: at sigma=10 it needs roughly 137 episodes per arm (one-sided 0.05, 80% power). 'Non-inferiority not contradicted' will therefore pass almost anything. Reframe it as a gross-harm check with a pre-stated detectable harm (for example 10 points or more) and report it as such.

Compliance gate item (ii) ('no statistic cutpoints') is broader than the rules. competition-rules.rst allows guidance such as 'consider low health', and the SKILL.md quality rubric rewards concrete decision criteria near limits. Restrict the ban to values searched or tuned on dev outcomes, and allow thresholds fixed in advance on published scales, stated as team margins.

Minor: 'Lost in the Middle' is a weak source for mid-episode instruction drift. Li et al. 2024 COLM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10962) and Laban et al. 2025 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120) fit better. The R40 'scanned image' premise behind 're-read SPS99 from a text copy' is false: the PDF has a text layer.

audit.dimension: Rules and compliance (permissions, scoring, models, deliverables, deadlines) for the hierarchical strategy lab
audit.verdict_summary: Most of what the package says about the rules is accurate. The scoring arithmetic (80/10/10, 56/7/7/30, competition_partial_score), the 500k tokens/month (24M per run) efficiency boundary, the cutoff conversions (24:00 GMT equals 00:00 on 28 Oct, 31 Oct and 2 Nov), the video requirement, the key restrictions, the ban on team mode and leader/teammate designs, and the ban on hard-coded answers regardless of how they were obtained all match the official docs. The 'silence is not permission' rule is also read correctly. The serious problems are operational and about how activities are labelled. First, the organiser question that gates the whole lab has not been sent. It is ten questions long and does not propose concrete limits, even though organisers only reply during working hours and the first cutoff is 24:00 GMT on 27 Oct. Second, no document gates the lab on the preliminary submission and competition key, although the preliminary files were deleted from the repo and the key has not arrived. Without the key the team cannot run the target actor or confirm that any submission was tested with JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3, and the docs require that confirmation. Third, two activities the docs do not address have already happened and are treated as ordinary evidence with no compliance caveat. One is the 73,858-game scripted random batch. The other is a dev game played by an AI assistant through Matteo's browser adapter, which is mislabelled as 'manual' play and justified by the user's authorisation instead of the organisers'. Fourth, the lab spec departs from the published scoring in two ways. It censors every interruption, but the official scoring gives any early exit a score from the state at exit, caps its token term at 50 and gives 0 when the token count is missing. It also uses quantitative_score alone as the primary metric, which ignores the token-efficiency term that depends on the policy. Fifth, the protocol paraphrases the MCP page as allowing other MCP clients without the stdio-only qualifier, and the current task plan includes an HTTP transport. Finally, the API price tables are the wrong cost model for the planned Claude Max subscription route.

errors.location: research/hierarchical-lab/lab-spec.json evaluation.unit ('administrative interruption is censored, not a score'); protocol.md §7 L93, §9 L132
errors.claim: Interruptions are censored and never scored.
errors.problem: Correct for faults in the lab's own infrastructure, but wrong for the target actor under the official runner. Official scoring gives any early exit a quantitative_score from the state at exit, caps its token term at 50, and gives 0 on that term when token or survival counts are missing. The intent is to stop early exits from outscoring completed runs. If the agent stops calling tools, hits an iteration or context limit, or crashes, that is an outcome of the policy and the organisers will score it. Censoring it biases the lab towards fragile, long-context policies.
errors.correction: Use four outcome classes: (i) game termination, scored; (ii) agent- or harness-intrinsic early stop under the official configuration, scored at state-at-exit with token term at most 50, or 0 if no counts; (iii) lab-infrastructure fault, censored and re-run, never zero; (iv) provider or key outage, censored but counted until the organisers answer (organiser-questions C9).

errors.claim: Primary outcome = mean terminal quantitative_score under the target actor.
errors.problem: The scored quantity is 0.8·mean(Q) + 0.1·DQ + 0.1·TE, and TE depends on the policy (tokens per month survived, cap at 50 on early exit). TE can only be measured with deepseek-v4-flash in JiuwenSwarm; token counts from Claude workers say nothing about it.
errors.correction: Pre-register the primary outcome as the projected automated score A_hat = 0.8·Q̄ + 0.1·TĒ + 0.1·DQ, with DQ held fixed or rubric-rated. Compute it only on target-actor runs. On cheap actors use Q as a proxy and treat target tokens per month as a separately estimated covariate.

audit.concrete_protocol:
ACTIVITY CLASSIFICATION, using the official docs only.

(a) Clearly permitted now:
- Programmatic MCP development client connected over STDIO to the unmodified career-emulator-engine-mcp, using only the five tools and the logs resource (mcp.rst 'Connecting another MCP client'). This covers the connection itself; who makes the choices is a separate question (see b1, b2).
- Official-runner runs with deepseek-v4-flash via the organiser key in JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3, mode agent, run sequentially. Volume is limited only by the USD 50 credit (api-key.rst: development and evaluation use is permitted; repeated runs are anticipated).
- Human manual play through the public CLI.
- Retaining your own run outputs (transcript-*.log, events-*.jsonl, score_report.json). Never read, copy or commit career_emulator.sqlite3.
- Outcome-level quantitative analysis of your own runs (mean and variance of Q, survival, tokens per month, failure causes). The docs ask teams to design for consistency across runs, and video question 2 expects debugging from earlier logs.
- Claude as an offline author or editor of general Skill text based on public docs and your own outputs. The docs regulate submission content and interfaces, not authoring tools; it is still folded into the question at no cost.
- Skill mode switches based on visible state, trends or the public calendar structure (quarters, six-month reviews, 48 months), written qualitatively. The rules explicitly allow strategies such as considering low health or sustained low dignity.

(b) Not addressed by the docs; needs an organiser reply on Discord before use:
1. Deterministic or scripted actor playing dev games. Already done once: the 74k random batch, which must be disclosed.
2. Claude models on the personal subscription as development actors. Already done once: the browser session, which must be disclosed and paused.
3. Several server processes in parallel or several concurrent sessions per server, and any non-stdio transport (http, sse, streamable-http from --help).
4. Thousands or more dev episodes outside the official runner. Millions would be pointless anyway.
5. Self-funded deepseek-v4-flash. This conflicts with the instruction that .env values come 'from the organiser email only'.
6. Competition key in a non-JiuwenSwarm harness for deepseek-v4-flash. Recommendation: never do this; the runner covers the need.
7. Fitting quantitative models of hidden dynamics or thresholds, even for analysis only.
8. Your own numeric safety margins on published stat ranges inside Skills. Low risk if worded as the team's heuristic, never as the game's threshold.

(c) Prohibited:
- Reading packages, .data files or the sqlite DB; using a modified server; calling internal functions.
- Using the competition key for Claude or any other model.
- Team mode, or a submitted procedure that needs a leader and teammates.
- Provider routing settings.
- Editing run artifacts.
- Skills containing event-keyed answers, lookup tables, dev-learned thresholds, formulas or score weights (such as the 30/20/15/15/10/10 pilot weights) presented as rules, or calendar rules that mirror the dev event sequence.

ORGANISER QUESTION (English, about 170 words, send today):
"Hello, team Gradient Depression here. Before we use the development methods below, could you confirm yes or no for each? None would be in, or needed by, our submission, which remains single-agent JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 with the designated model.
1. Our own MCP client connects to the unmodified career-emulator-engine-mcp over stdio, uses only the five official tools, and plays dev games with (a) scripted non-LLM policies, or (b) Claude models on our own subscription (never the competition key).
2. Scale: at most 8 server processes in parallel; at most 20,000 scripted and 1,000 Claude-played dev games in total.
3. Claude used offline to analyse our own run outputs and edit general Skill text (no event-specific answers, no unpublished thresholds or formulas).
4. Extra deepseek-v4-flash dev runs in JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 with our own paid key.
Disclosure: a teammate already ran about 74,000 uniformly random dev games through such a client, and an AI assistant played one partial game through a local browser wrapper. Please tell us if either was not acceptable. Thank you!"

DECISION RULES ON THE REPLY:
- Yes to 1b and 2: enable Claude workers within the approved caps and log the message link.
- Yes to 1a only: use scripted actors only to validate the harness and statistics on real noise; the worker tier becomes deepseek via the runner.
- No, or no reply by 18:00 GMT on 27 Oct: the lab stays synthetic plus official-runner only.
- Generic reply: follow up quoting the caps; do not treat it as approval of scale or concurrency.
- Yes to 4: use self-funded deepseek runs as a separate environment epoch, since hosting may differ, and do not pool them with organiser-key runs without a check.

OUTCOME AND METRIC SPECIFICATION:
- Classes: (i) game termination, scored; (ii) agent- or harness-intrinsic early stop under the official configuration, Q taken at state-at-exit and token term ≤50, or 0 if counts are missing; (iii) lab-infrastructure fault, censored and re-run, never zero; (iv) provider or key outage, censored and counted.
- Primary metric, on target runs: A_hat = 0.8·mean(Q) + 0.1·mean(TE) + 0.1·DQ.
- TE = 100 if t ≤ 500k; 0 if t ≥ 3M; otherwise 100·(3M − t)/2.5M; capped at 50 if survival < 48; 0 if missing.
- Final-version choice: maximise E[max(S*, A)], where S* is the best score already issued.

WHAT CAN BE DONE NOW WITHOUT ANY CLARIFICATION:
1. Verify or upload the preliminary submission and chase the key.
2. Run make sync and the validation command in local-runs/official-runner. When the key arrives, run make setup, make start-jiuwen and a sequential make play / make score / make replay pilot, logging tokens per month, survival, Q, terminal cause and outcome class.
3. Build the registry, schema checks, pre-registered statistics and a synthetic testbed with known ground truth. Run baselines and ablations (diversity, reopening, calibration, specialisation) there.
4. Have Claude draft general candidate policies offline from public docs only.
5. Write and run the Skill compliance lint.
6. Prepare the cutoff-1 package: solution/ with an English manifest (real team name, mode agent), README, design/skills_design.md and decision_report.md, at least one SKILL.md, and a real person-on-camera presentation.mp4 of at most 10 minutes answering the five questions in order. Validate with `uv run python -m career_sim_runner validate --submission solution`, test with 0.2.4b3, and submit before 24:00 GMT on 27 Oct.
7. Human CLI play for familiarisation.

verdicts.reason: This is a gap in specification, not a contradiction. mathematics.md L126 already says a legitimate early exit is not silently excluded. With the current enum such runs would fall into censored or infrastructure_failure. competition-rules.rst says 'An early exit still receives one, from the state at exit', caps the token term at 50 for runs that end before month 48, and scores 0 when counts are missing. verdicts.reason: The arithmetic checks out. At 1M tokens/month, TE = 100*(3M-1M)/2.5M = 80, a loss of 2.0 automated points, against +0.8 for +1 Q, so the net is -1.2. lab-spec primary_outcome and registry E01-E03 primary_metric are Q only, but TE is policy-dependent, averaged per run, and capped at 50 on early exit. The research is not unaware of TE: experiment-plan.md L24 records tokens to 'compute published token efficiency', and mathematics.md L19 notes that optimising mu is one component of the score. The error is in which outcome was pre-registered as the decision metric.
verdicts.refined_correction: Pre-register A_hat = 0.8*mean(Q) + 0.1*mean(TE_r) + 0.1*DQ_fixed for target runs. TE_r follows the published piecewise rule, with a cap of 50 if survival < 48 and 0 if counts are missing. On cheap actors keep Q as the primary metric and model target tokens per month as a separate covariate. Report Q and TE alongside A_hat.

recommendation_objections: The auditor's disclosure is incomplete in the way it criticises. findings.md L44-47 (uncommitted, written today by this orchestrator) and careerlab/mcp_client.py L66-67 / diagnostics.py L36-40 show that CareerLab has already run streamable-http servers, 8 concurrent calls, a 48-episode scripted bench through one 16-way server, and session-eviction probes. The proposed organiser message and the 'already done' list name only Matteo's batch and the browser session. Disclosing only those while omitting the team's own HTTP and concurrency tests would misrepresent what has been done.

The classification contradicts itself. Class (a) says a 'programmatic MCP development client over STDIO' is clearly permitted, but (b1) puts a 'scripted actor' in the needs-a-reply class. A programmatic client must be choosing actions somehow, by script or by LLM. mcp.rst allows development clients without restricting how they choose. The real uncertainties are volume, concurrency, and non-designated LLM actors. The blanket 'stop all scripted activity' in recommendation 3 also blocks a few sequential stdio games for harness validation, which the auditor's own class (a) appears to allow.

The caps in the question (8 parallel processes, 20,000 scripted games, 1,000 Claude-played games) are not derived from need or from measured usage. That contradicts recommendation 11, 'measure usage per episode in a pilot before setting any fleet size'. findings.md L48 reports that the claude CLI on this Mac is logged in as Pro with 79% of its 7-day quota used. Anthropic's legal page (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) says Max/Pro limits 'assume ordinary, individual usage'. Asking for 1,000 Claude games is unrealistic and makes a 'no' more likely. Ask for small caps tied to the pilot design instead.

Recommendation 4 does not deliver isolation. findings.md L44 shows that processes without CAREER_EMULATOR_DB share one default store even across working directories, and L46 shows that about 20 sessions are retained per database, with active sessions evicted. Isolating each worker requires a separate CAREER_EMULATOR_DB per process. The docs do not mention that variable; only the official runner's setup.py uses it. By the auditor's own strict standard it belongs in the question, or execution should be serialised to one database.

The proposed question drops B4 and B5 from the existing draft (quantitative modelling of own transitions; qualitative learning across own runs; cross-game memory in official evaluation). Yet the auditor's own (b7) and (b8) list those as needing a reply. Either ask them as yes/no items or stop classifying them as blocked.

Disclosing Matteo's batch should be agreed with Matteo first, together with a check on whether he already asked the organisers; no repo evidence settles that. The description should be accurate: a scripted client through the local adapter to the official server over stdio, without the runner's environment settings.

The decision rule 'no reply by 18:00 GMT 27 Oct -> synthetic plus official runner only' should not close off later approval. Replies can still arrive on Wed-Fri (28-30 Oct) during working hours. Make it a default that is revisited on each reply.

Recommendation 8's E[max(S*, A)] criterion ignores that the real objective is first a top-10 rank (P(max >= threshold)) and then 0.7*Stage1 + 0.3*expert review, which draws on the final ZIP's documents and video. Final-release scores also arrive only after the week, so S* is at most the best interim score. Use the probability of exceeding a top-10 threshold, plus consistency of the design documents, as a joint criterion.

Recommendation 10's rationale over-reads packages.rst: its rejection of substituted versions is about JiuwenSwarm, not FastMCP. Treating Matteo's FastMCP 4.1.3 environment as a separate epoch is still prudent. The stronger reason is findings.md L39: the adapter set none of the runner's server environment variables (event limits, chain limit, note length), so its dynamics may differ.

audit.dimension: Teammate evidence and exploration claims (origin/Matteo 0eb0924 and 27cd3c1, as audited in matteo-branch-review.md, from-zero-lab.md, experiment-registry.json, RESUMEN_ES.md and experiment-plan.md)
audit.verdict_summary: The repo reports the teammate's numbers correctly, and its caution is mostly justified. Every figure in matteo-branch-review.md matches docs/experiments/random-baseline-summary.json, which is unchanged at 27cd3c1. The derived arithmetic is right: the causes sum to 73,858, the other causes total 2,803, Blackout plus Trust crisis is 96.2049%, there are 21.17 actions per session, and throughput is 5.129 sessions/s. Further consistency checks the review did not run also pass: summed survival is exactly 436,174 months, and summed score is 870,354.9 at a 0.1 resolution. The competing-risks caveat is correct, and so is the description of 27cd3c1 as an unbenchmarked three-Skill candidate. The main weaknesses lie elsewhere. (1) Information the aggregates do carry goes unused: a Bhatia-Davis bound on variance (SE of the random mean is at most 0.045), a measured 3.58 decisions per survived month, and about 108 actions/s of sequential engine throughput. (2) The first registered experiment, E01, contradicts the review's own competing-risks caveat: it takes its factors (health x risk feedback) from random-play terminal causes and pushes growth back to E03, which builds in the early-filter bias (problem B). (3) Three plans for the same USD 50 key have not been reconciled: the teammate's 100-run single-candidate target, the roughly 30-game multi-arm plan, and the USD 5/15/15/10/5 split in RESUMEN_ES. (4) The team's stance on compliance has gaps. The draft organiser questions treat a non-LLM automated driver as hypothetical when a 73,858-session driver has already run, and a would-be deliverable (decision_report.md) cites that batch. Separately, the preliminary package the API key depends on was deleted, and no file says whether it was ever submitted. (5) Several documents are stale, and the records lack provenance: the registry has no entry for v0.1 or the Codex exercise, no environment versions, and nobody noted that FastMCP 4.1.3 falls outside the official runner's fastmcp>=2,<3 pin. Sustainable Career v0.1 is compliant: no named-event answers and no unpublished thresholds. It is a reasonable incumbent, a balanced 'triage, then growth' generalist with an honesty preference in story choices. But it bundles at least five changes at once, so it can show which policy to pick but cannot show which change helped. A fair test needs the target actor, an operational-hygiene control, a one-file packaging ablation, interleaved runs to real termination, and sample sizes driven by observed variance. The random baseline is legitimately a floor reference and a client-conformance target in its own environment, plus a prior on decisions per game. It is not a priority ranking, not a variance prior for reasoned policies, not usable for off-policy evaluation, and beyond serving as a 'null actor' it is no calibration anchor.
